In 1927, tire mogul Harvey Firestone gifted a pygmy hippopotamus named Billy to President Calvin Coolidge, and Billy became the genetic ancestor of almost every pygmy hippo in American zoos.

Unlike common hippos with eyes and nostrils perched atop the head for floating, pygmy hippopotamuses have eyes on the sides of their skulls and sloped backs made for ducking through dense forest undergrowth.
Bat-eared fox: Bat-eared foxes possess up to 50 teeth, more than almost any other land mammal, with tiny, specialized molars built to pulverize tough insect exoskeletons.

A bat-eared fox's five-inch-tall ears are packed with a dense network of blood vessels that shed excess body heat while amplifying the faint crunch of subterranean beetle larvae chewing roots a foot underground.
A special muscle attachment in a bat-eared fox's lower jaw lets it open and snap its mouth shut five times per second like a rapid-fire staple gun.
A single bat-eared fox consumes over 1.15 million harvester termites a year, getting nearly all of its daily water directly from the body fluids of its prey.
Among bat-eared foxes, fathers do the majority of the parenting, guarding the den, grooming the pups, and taking them on their very first foraging trips while the mother rests.
Weasel: Weasels perform a frantic 'weasel war dance' of erratic flips, sideways hops, and somersaults to confuse and hypnotize rabbits before delivering a lightning-fast bite to the neck.
Weasels' long, tubular bodies lose body heat rapidly, so they have a furnace-like metabolism and must eat up to half their own body weight every single day just to stay alive.
In snowy regions, a weasel's brown summer coat molts into pure white 'ermine' fur, except for a jet-black tail tip designed to trick diving hawks into striking at the tail instead of the head.
A least weasel can squeeze through a hole no wider than a wedding ring and routinely raids underground mouse tunnels that are completely inaccessible to larger predators.
Despite weighing less than a candy bar, the least weasel routinely takes down prey up to ten times its own size, including full-grown hares.
Jerboa: A jerboa's hind feet have fused cannon bones, three separate foot bones melted into one solid rod, acting as shock-absorbing pogo sticks that let it leap up to ten feet in a single bound.
The tufts of stiff hair on the bottoms of a jerboa's feet work just like snowshoes, preventing it from sinking into loose desert sand and kicking dust into predators' faces.
Wait-time in pregnancy is flexible for some jerboas, which enter deep winter hibernation and emerge to mate using an internal biological clock triggered by soil temperature.
The long-eared jerboa boasts ears that are up to two-thirds the length of its entire body, making its ears proportionally larger than an African elephant's.
During World War II, the British 7th Armoured Division in North Africa adopted the jerboa as their emblem and became famously known as the 'Desert Rats.'
Harbor seal: While lounging on rocky shores, harbor seals hold their heads and hind flippers high in the air in a curved 'banana pose' to regulate body temperature and keep dry until the tide rises.
Before diving up to 1,500 feet deep, a harbor seal actually exhales to empty its lungs, preventing decompression sickness ('the bends') and storing oxygen directly in its thick, dark blood instead.

A harbor seal's beaded, wavy whiskers, called vibrissae, are so sensitive to hydrodynamic water trails that a blindfolded seal can track the exact size and direction of a fish that swam past 30 seconds earlier.
Unlike almost all other mammals, harbor seal pups shed their fluffy white lanugo coat inside their mother's womb before birth, enabling them to swim within minutes of being born.

In the 1970s and 80s, an orphaned harbor seal in Maine named Hoover learned to mimic human speech in a thick New England fisherman's accent, shouting 'Hey! How are ya?' and 'Get outta there!' at aquarium visitors.
Galago: Also known as bushbabies because a galago's eerie nighttime cries sound just like a wailing human infant, they can jump over six feet straight up in the air powered by elastic tendons in their ankles.
A galago's enormous eyes are so large and tubular that they are locked completely in place within their sockets; to look around, it must swivel its entire head like an owl.

Galagos practice 'urine washing,' deliberately peeing onto their hands and rubbing the urine onto the soles of their feet to improve their grip on slick branches and leave a scent trail with every leap.
A galago possesses a second, spiky 'sub-tongue' hidden underneath its main tongue, which works with comb-like lower front teeth to scrape sticky tree gum and clean matted fur.
While flying through pitch-black branches in mid-air, galagos fold their delicate, bat-like ears completely flat against their heads to shield them from twigs and thorns.
American badger: American badgers and coyotes have been filmed teaming up as hunting partners; the badger digs into squirrel burrows from below while the coyote waits at the escape holes above.

Armed with two-inch curved front claws and loose neck skin that lets American badgers twist around and bite even while pinned in a predator's jaws, they can dig themselves completely underground in less than a minute.
Female American badgers use 'delayed implantation,' mating in mid-summer but pausing the fertilized egg's development until the dead of winter so their cubs are born in the warmth of spring.
To preserve food in the summer heat, an American badger will bury a slain ground squirrel or prairie dog completely underground in a cool, custom-dug pantry tunnel.
The American badger did not actually inspire Wisconsin's nickname 'The Badger State'; the name came from 1820s lead miners who dug cave-like shelters into hillsides instead of building houses.
Marmoset: Nearly every marmoset pregnancy produces fraternal twins that share a fused placenta in the womb, swapping stem cells so that each sibling carries the other's DNA in its blood and organs for life.

Marmoset fathers and older brothers carry the newborn twins on their backs almost continuously, experiencing spikes in prolactin, the hormone associated with nursing, and losing up to 10 percent of their body weight from the effort.
Pygmy marmosets can weigh less than a single AA battery, clinging vertically to tree trunks and chiseling rows of tiny holes into the bark so they can return the next day to lap up the sap.
Young marmosets go through a babbling phase just like human babies, stringing together random chirps, trills, and whistles until their parents respond and shape their vocalizations into adult calls.
Instead of flat fingernails like most primates, marmosets have sharp, claw-like nails called tegulae on every digit except their big toes, allowing them to scamper up smooth tree bark like squirrels.
American pika: Because American pikas do not hibernate, they spend the entire summer building giant 'haypiles' of up to 60 pounds of wildflowers and grasses under rocks to sustain them under the winter snowpack.

American pikas are savvy organic chemists: they intentionally harvest toxic alpine plants filled with natural preservatives that won't rot, storing them until the poison breaks down in late winter and the plants become safe to eat.

An American pika's resting body temperature is dangerously close to its lethal limit, around 104°F, meaning that just a few hours trapped in temperatures above 78°F without cool shade can cause fatal heatstroke.
Like rabbits, American pikas produce two distinct types of droppings, immediately eating the soft, shiny green 'cecotropes' straight from their bodies to extract B vitamins and protein a second time.
Even the soles of an American pika's feet are covered in dense fur, giving them both insulation on freezing snow and traction when leaping across slick granite boulders.
Gemsbok: Despite gemsboks standing under scorching Kalahari sun where their body temperature climbs past 113°F, a specialized network of blood vessels called the carotid rete cools blood flowing to their brain by several degrees so they don't suffer brain damage.
Both male and female gemsboks wield rapier-straight, ringed horns up to nearly four feet long, and females actually have longer, thinner horns that are even deadlier for skewering attacking lions.

When viewed in profile from a distance, a standing gemsbok's two horns align so perfectly that they look like a single horn, a visual illusion widely believed to have inspired early traveler myths of the unicorn.
Gemsboks can sniff out buried desert melons and water-storing tubers deeply hidden beneath dry sand, digging them up with their hooves to survive months without surface water.
A gemsbok's striking black-and-white Kabuki-style facial markings help herd members communicate gaze direction and head posture across shimmering desert heat mirages.
Striped skunk: Before firing a notorious spray, a striped skunk always gives a three-step polite warning: it stomps its front paws loudly, hisses while raising its tail, and sometimes pops up into a handstand.
A striped skunk's dual anal scent glands act like twin squirt guns with directional nozzles that can accurately hit a target between the eyes from up to 15 feet away.

Striped skunk spray contains sulfur compounds called thiols that are so flammable and pungent the human nose can detect them at concentrations of just 10 parts per billion, and it takes up to 10 days for a skunk to fully recharge its empty glands.
Striped skunks are functionally immune to rattlesnake and copperhead venom, allowing them to casually hunt and eat venomous pit vipers without getting sick.
Great horned owls are the striped skunk's top natural predator simply because the owls have almost no sense of smell and aren't bothered in the slightest by being sprayed.
South American tapir: A South American tapir's flexible snout is actually a fusion of the nose and upper lip that works as a prehensile snorkel, grabbing high leaves on land and breathing above the surface while the tapir walks along riverbeds underwater.

Born looking like walking watermelons, baby South American tapirs sport a dark coat covered in white stripes and spots that mimic dappled forest sunlight until the camouflage fades at around six months of age.
With four toes on a South American tapir's front feet and three on its back feet, its splayed hooves work like mud-shoes on soft riverbanks.

Known as the 'gardeners of the forest,' a single South American tapir swallows thousands of large fruit seeds whole and deposits them in nutrient-rich dung piles inside rivers and clearings across miles of territory.

Male South American tapirs boast one of the largest penises relative to body size of any land mammal, which actually features flared, gripping lobes at the tip to ensure successful mating in the water.
Flying squirrel: Under ultraviolet blacklight, flying squirrels glow a vibrant neon bubble-gum pink due to porphyrin compounds in their fur, a secret visual signal visible to nocturnal owls and fellow squirrels.

Flying squirrels possess a special wrist spur of cartilage called the styliform cartilage that pops out like a switchblade when they leap, stretching their furry gliding membrane tight and acting as a winglet to reduce air drag.

Flying squirrels never truly flap to fly, yet a flying squirrel can glide over the length of a football field from a single tall tree, using its flat, feathery tail as a rudder to make mid-air 90-degree turns.
In freezing winter weather, up to 20 otherwise solitary flying squirrels will pack tightly into a single woodpecker cavity to share body heat, raising the nest's temperature by more than 50°F.
A flying squirrel, right before slamming into a tree trunk at the end of a glide, flips its body upward to stall like a parachute and lands softly on all four shock-absorbing paws.
Red kangaroo: At high speeds, a red kangaroo actually uses less energy the faster it hops because its giant Achilles tendons stretch and snap back like rubber bands, while the bouncing of its internal organs pumps air in and out of its lungs like a piston.

A female red kangaroo can be perpetually pregnant, simultaneously nursing an older joey outside the pouch, a tiny hairless joey attached to a teat inside the pouch, and holding a third fertilized embryo in suspended animation.

A mother red kangaroo can produce two completely different formulas of milk at the exact same time from two separate teats: one high-fat milk for the older joey and one high-carbohydrate milk for the newborn.

During heatwaves, red kangaroos lick their own forearms until they are soaking wet; a dense patch of superficial blood vessels right beneath the skin cools their entire bloodstream as the saliva evaporates.
When moving slowly while grazing, a red kangaroo uses its muscular tail as a 'fifth leg,' planting it on the ground to support its entire body weight while swinging both hind legs forward together.
Tiger quoll: Despite being the size of a housecat, the tiger quoll possesses the second-strongest bite force relative to body size of any living mammal on Earth, trailing only its cousin, the Tasmanian devil.

A mother tiger quoll gives birth to up to 30 rice-grain-sized joeys at once, even though her backward-facing pouch only has six teats, creating a ruthless race where only the first six babies to latch on survive.
Unlike almost all other marsupials, tiger quolls establish communal 'latrine sites' on flat rocky ledges where every quoll in the area deposits its droppings to leave social updates for neighbors.

Ridged, fleshy pads on the bottoms of a tiger quoll's paws and a fully opposable hallux (thumb-toe) on its hind feet allow it to climb smooth eucalyptus trunks and ambush sleeping possums and gliders in the canopy.
During the brief mid-winter mating season, female tiger quolls develop swollen necks to survive the famously rough courtship bites of males that clamp onto their shoulders for hours.
Chamois: Before synthetic microfiber was invented, 'shammy' leather cloths used for polishing cars without scratching paint were genuinely made from the oil-tanned hide of the alpine chamois.
A chamois's hooves have a hard, sharp outer rim surrounding a soft, spongy inner pad that acts like a suction cup on wet, icy limestone cliffs.
A chamois can leap nearly 20 feet horizontally across mountain chasms and bound up near-vertical rock faces at speeds topping 30 miles per hour.
In winter, male chamois grow a prized tuft of eight-inch-long hair along their spine called the 'Gamsbart' (chamois beard), which traditional Alpine hunters wear as an expensive plume on their hats.

Both male and female chamois carry backward-curved, fishhook-shaped black horns that they use not just for headbutting rivals, but for hooking an opponent's legs or belly from underneath on steep ledges.
Vervet monkey: Vervet monkeys use distinct vocabulary words for different predators: a 'leopard' alarm sends the troop scrambling into the highest thin tree branches, an 'eagle' call makes them dive into low bushes, and a 'snake' call makes everyone stand on their hind legs and peer into the grass.

Adult male vervet monkeys display a bright turquoise-blue scrotum framed by a vivid scarlet-red penis and brilliant white belly fur, and the shade of blue actually fades if a dominant male loses social status in the troop.

On the Caribbean island of St. Kitts, where escaped vervet monkeys have lived since the 1600s, scientists studying them discovered the monkeys voluntarily raid beach bars to drink leftover cocktails in exact proportion to human drinking patterns (some teetotalers, most social drinkers, and a few heavy binge drinkers).
High-ranking vervet monkey mothers get preferential babysitting from lower-ranking females eager to curry favor and gain grooming privileges within the troop's strict matriarchal hierarchy.
When crossing open ground between patches of trees, vervet monkeys often walk upright on two legs so they can carry stolen farm crops in both hands while keeping watch over tall grass.
Babirusa: In male babirusas, the upper canine teeth never enter the mouth at all; instead, they grow upside-down straight through the flesh and bone of the top of the snout, curving backward toward the eyes.

If a male babirusa does not wear down or snap off his ever-growing upper tusks by rubbing them against trees, the tusks can eventually curl all the way back and pierce right through his own skull and brain.
Babirusas' curving upper tusks are actually quite brittle, so battling babirusa males don't slash each other; instead, they rear up on their hind legs and box like kangaroos with their front hooves.

The babirusa has a soft nose and can only forage in loose mud, rotting logs, and fallen fruit, unlike every other wild pig species, which have tough rostral bones in their snouts for rooting up hard earth.

The babirusa's digestive tract features an enlarged fore-stomach more like a sheep's or hippo's than a typical pig's, leading local Indonesian folklore to view babirusas as half-pig, half-deer (the name literally translates to 'pig-deer').
Ibex: In Northern Italy, Alpine ibexes regularly scale the near-vertical 160-foot stone wall of the Cingino Dam on hooves the width of a human thumb just to lick mineral salts seeping from the masonry.

Male ibexes carry scimitar-shaped, heavily ridged horns that can reach nearly five feet in length and weigh over 30 pounds, and during fights, they rear up on their hind legs to slam those horns down with a crack audible a mile away.

In the Middle Ages, powdered ibex horn and 'bezoar stones' from an ibex's stomach were worth their weight in gold as supposed cure-alls for poison, driving the species to the brink of extinction until a single Italian king protected the last 100 survivors in 1821.
An ibex's split hooves operate independently like pincers, gripping tiny rock seams less than an inch wide while soft, rubbery heel pads conform to uneven granite.
Every single living Alpine ibex today is descended from that tiny royal herd kept in Italy's Gran Paradiso mountains in the 19th century.
Elephant shrew: Despite looking like a mouse with a miniature anteater snout, DNA studies revealed that elephant shrews are not rodents or shrews at all; their closest living relatives include elephants, manatees, and aardvarks.

Elephant shrews spend hours every day maintaining a meticulous network of tiny, swept 'highways' through the leaf litter, clearing away every twig and pebble so they can sprint away from predators at nearly 18 miles per hour without tripping.
A giant elephant shrew's tongue is so long it extends past the tip of its flexible trunk-like nose, allowing it to flick ants and termites into its mouth while keeping its snout in constant motion.

Monogamous elephant shrew pairs share the exact same territory for life, yet they rarely hang out together; each partner patrols the shared highway network solo and only meets up briefly to mate or defend the border.

When startled, elephant shrews drum their long hind feet rapidly against dry leaves to broadcast a seismic and acoustic vibration that tells snakes and lizards, 'I've already spotted you, don't bother chasing me.'
Muntjac: Known as the 'barking deer,' an alarmed muntjac can bark continuously for over an hour with a sharp, hoarse yip that sounds almost indistinguishable from a medium-sized dog.

Muntjacs can open their faces like a transformer: four large scent glands on their forehead and beneath their eyes literally turn inside out and inflate into fleshy pockets when the deer marks branches or courts a mate.
Male muntjacs are armed with both small branched antlers and razor-sharp, downward-pointing upper canine tusks, using their antlers to parry a rival's head and then slashing with their fangs.
The Indian muntjac holds the record for the lowest chromosome count of any mammal on Earth; females have just six chromosomes and males have seven, compared to 46 in humans.
After a handful of Reeves's muntjacs escaped from Woburn Abbey in 1925, they quietly colonized the British countryside and are now one of the most widespread wild mammals in England.
Proboscis monkey: An adult male proboscis monkey's pendulous, eggplant-shaped nose can grow past four inches long, hanging down over his mouth so that he physically has to push it aside with his hand to eat certain foods.
A male proboscis monkey's oversized nose acts as a natural echo chamber, amplifying his honks and roars across dense mangrove swamps to intimidate rivals and attract females.

Proboscis monkeys have partially webbed hands and feet and are the most aquatic of all primates, frequently belly-flopping off branches 50 feet high into crocodile-infested rivers and swimming up to 65 feet completely underwater.

A proboscis monkey's permanent 'pot belly' isn't fat; it's a massive, four-chambered cow-like stomach packed with symbiotic bacteria that ferment toxic mangrove leaves and unripe fruit, making up a quarter of the monkey's entire body weight.
Eating sweet, ripe fruit can actually kill a proboscis monkey; the sugars ferment so rapidly inside their specialized stomachs that they cause fatal, balloon-like bloating.
Spinner dolphin: Spinner dolphins are the only cetaceans that can spin like a drill bit in mid-air, launching ten feet above the waves and completing up to seven full body rotations in a single leap before splashing back down.

Spinner dolphins' spinning leaps aren't just for fun, scientists found; the torque of spinning in the air followed by a loud belly-flop strips off parasitic remora suckerfish and broadcasts an acoustic ping to keep the pod together at night.

Spinner dolphins, like other dolphins, sleep with only half their brain at a time, swimming slowly in tight, synchronized formations with one eye open to watch for sharks and remember to surface for air.

In Hawaiian waters, spinner dolphins hunt deep-water squid and lanternfish all night long, then spend their mornings resting over bright white sand flats so the pale seafloor makes dark shark silhouettes instantly visible.
An adult spinner dolphin can pack up to 260 tiny, needle-sharp interlocking teeth into its long, slender beak; more teeth than almost any other dolphin species.
Agouti: The agouti is virtually the only animal in the Amazon rainforest with chisel-like front teeth strong enough to gnaw open the rock-hard, cannonball-sized seed pods of the Brazil nut tree.
Because agoutis bury surplus Brazil nuts one by one across the forest floor and forget where they hid many of them, huge commercial Brazil nut trees cannot reproduce in the wild without wild agoutis.
When eating, an agouti sits upright on its haunches and holds fruit or nuts between its front paws just like an oversized squirrel, peeling away the tough rind before eating the flesh.
If threatened, the agouti erects a dramatic fan of long, coarse hairs on its rump and leaps up to six feet straight into the air while letting out a piercing alarm bark.

Although monogamous agouti pairs stay together until one partner dies, the male isn't allowed near the burrow when babies are born; the fiercely protective mother chases him off until the precocial pups are ready to forage.
Kudu: A male greater kudu's corkscrew horns take six full years to complete their two-and-a-half twists, and if straightened out, a single horn could reach nearly six feet in length.
Sometimes two sparring male kudus lock their spiraling horns together so tightly that neither animal can pull free, resulting in both rivals dying together of exhaustion.
Despite standing five feet tall at the shoulder and weighing up to 700 pounds, a kudu can effortlessly clear an eight-foot-high ranch fence from a nearly standing start.
Traditional African sportsmen and scouts have long blown hollowed-out kudu horns as deep, resonant 'vuvuzelas' and ceremonial trumpets whose low notes carry for miles across the bushveld.

When hiding in dry woodland, a kudu freezes completely motionless; the vertical white stripes down its flanks break up its outline so effectively that predators can walk within yards without seeing it.
Honduran white bat: Measuring less than two inches long, Honduran white bats are tiny snow-white puffballs that chew the side veins of giant Heliconia leaves until the leaf collapses into a waterproof, V-shaped tent.

As sunlight filters through the green leaf tent from above, a Honduran white bat's pure white fur reflects the green glow, rendering the huddled colony nearly invisible to predators looking up from the forest floor.

Honduran white bats are one of the only mammals on Earth able to accumulate bright yellow carotenoid pigments (lutein) in their skin, giving their noses, ears, and wings a vivid marigold-orange color.

Up to a dozen Honduran white bats, usually one adult male and a harem of females, roost pressed tightly in a single line along a leaf's central rib, ready to burst out into flight the instant a snake vibrates the stem.
Unlike almost all other small bats that hunt insects, Honduran white bats are strict fruit specialists that feed almost exclusively on a single species of wild fig.
Warthog: Despite a warthog's fierce tusks, its facial 'warts' aren't blemishes or skin growths at all; they are thick, cartilaginous crash pads that protect the eyes and jawbones during high-speed tusk battles.

When retreating into an abandoned aardvark burrow for the night, a warthog always backs in rear-end first so its razor-sharp lower tusks are facing the doorway ready to gore any leopard or hyena that tries to follow.
To reach short, sweet grass shoots without bending a warthog's short neck, it drops down onto calloused, padded wrists and shuffles across the savanna on its knees.

At the crack of dawn, warthogs explode out of their burrows at full sprint in case a predator is waiting outside to ambush them, a behavior that occasionally sends waiting lions flying through the air.
While fleeing danger, an entire warthog family runs in single file with their tufted tails held straight up in the air like radio antennas so the piglets can follow the herd through tall grass.
Squirrel monkey: The squirrel monkey holds the highest brain-to-body mass ratio of any primate, about 1:17, which is roughly twice the brain-to-body ratio of a human being.

In 1959, a Peruvian squirrel monkey named Miss Baker rode a Jupiter rocket 300 miles into space and returned safely, going on to live for another 25 years on a diet of bananas, cottage cheese, and strawberry gelatin.

During the annual two-month breeding season, adult male squirrel monkeys transform into 'fatted males,' rapidly gaining up to 25 percent of their body weight in water and fat around their shoulders and arms to look more impressive to females.
Because squirrel monkeys cannot sweat through their body skin, they keep cool in the humid canopy by urinating on their hands and feet and letting the moisture evaporate as they climb.

Adult squirrel monkeys use their long, black-tipped tails strictly as a balancing pole rather than hanging from branches like larger South American monkeys, though infants curl their tails around their mother's back like a seatbelt.
Tree-kangaroo: Unlike ground-dwelling kangaroos, tree-kangaroos can move their hind legs independently to walk and climb, and they always climb down tree trunks backward.
Tree-kangaroos can leap down from canopy branches as high as 60 feet to the forest floor without suffering a single injury, using their heavy, furry tails as a counterbalance.
Tree-kangaroos' sponge-like, rubbery paw pads and curved claws act like natural climbing cleats to grip slippery, moss-covered bark in cloud forests.
Tree-kangaroos' diet of tough leaves is slow to digest, so they have a multi-chambered stomach full of fermenting bacteria, much like a cow.
Matschie's tree-kangaroos stay completely dry in torrential rainforest downpours thanks to a whorl of hair on their backs that channels rainwater right off their coats.
Kangaroo rat: A kangaroo rat can go its entire life without ever drinking a single drop of liquid water, manufacturing all the moisture it needs metabolically from dry seeds.
A kangaroo rat's kidneys are roughly five times more efficient than a human's, producing urine so concentrated that it crystallizes almost immediately after hitting the ground.
To escape ambushing rattlesnakes in pitch darkness, the kangaroo rat has oversized, hollow middle-ear chambers that can detect the low-frequency rustle of a snake's scales before the strike finishes.
Wait-time in midair is no problem for a kangaroo rat: it can flick its long tail mid-leap to change direction in flight and kick sand directly into a rattlesnake's eyes.
Inside a kangaroo rat's long nasal passages, cooler tissue condenses moisture from every exhaled breath so the animal reabsorbs water just by breathing.
Mountain goat: The mountain goat is not actually a true goat at all, but a member of the goat-antelope group more closely related to the European chamois and Asian takin.
Each of a mountain goat's hooves features a hard outer rim surrounding a soft, rubbery inner pad that conforms to tiny rock ledges like the sole of a high-friction climbing shoe.
With a single bound, a mountain goat can jump nearly 12 feet laterally across sheer cliff faces while pulling its body weight up with powerful shoulder muscles.
Mountain goats' dense, double-layered white coats can withstand freezing winds of 100 miles per hour and temperatures plunging to minus 50 degrees Fahrenheit.
Dominant mountain goat nannies are fiercely territorial over mineral licks and will even chase off subordinate billies to secure salt for themselves and their kids.
Pine marten: Pine martens have semi-retractable claws and ultra-flexible ankle joints that can rotate 180 degrees, allowing them to run straight down vertical tree trunks headfirst.

In parts of Ireland and Scotland, resurgent pine marten populations have naturally restored native red squirrels because heavier, less agile invasive gray squirrels are much easier for martens to catch.
A female pine marten can delay the implantation of fertilized eggs for nearly seven months, mating in mid-summer so her kits are born safely the following spring.
Instead of digging burrows from scratch, pine martens keep up to a dozen different hollow-tree and rock-crevice dens across their territory and rotate between them nightly.
Despite being fierce woodland hunters, pine martens develop a serious sweet tooth in late summer and will gorge on bilberries, rowan berries, and stolen honey.
Malayan tapir: Although an adult Malayan tapir looks stark and unmistakable with its two-tone black-and-white 'saddle' coat, that bold pattern actually acts as disruptive camouflage by breaking up its outline in moonlit forests.
Baby Malayan tapirs look nothing like their parents, arriving covered in chocolate-brown fur patterned with white stripes and spots like a furry watermelon.
A Malayan tapir's flexible snout is a true prehensile proboscis made of muscle and soft tissue that it uses both to pluck leaves and as a snorkel while walking underwater along riverbeds.
When startled, a Malayan tapir can defend itself by spraying a powerful, foul-smelling jet of urine backward up to several feet.
Often called living fossils, Malayan tapirs have kept almost the exact same body plan for over 30 million years and are most closely related to horses and rhinoceroses.
Bongo: Unlike almost all other spiral-horned antelopes, both male and female bongos grow long, lyre-shaped horns that twist in a full spiral.
When running through dense tangles of jungle vines, a bongo tilts its chin up so its long horns lie flat along its back, preventing them from snagging on branches.
After lightning storms in the forest, bongos purposefully seek out burned trees and chew on the charred wood and ash to get vital salts and minerals.
The white vertical stripes along a bongo's rich chestnut coat mimic shafts of sunlight filtering through dense forest foliage, making a standing bongo nearly invisible.
Local folklore in parts of Central Africa once held the bongo in such awe that villagers believed touching one or eating its meat would cause neurological spasms.
Pocket gopher: A pocket gopher's fur-lined cheek pouches are actually on the outside of its cheeks and can be turned completely inside out like pant pockets to shake out dirt.
A pocket gopher's lips close tightly behind its four large front incisor teeth, so it can chew straight through hard roots and packed soil without getting a mouthful of dirt.
A pocket gopher's front teeth grow up to 14 inches a year to compensate for the relentless wear of chiseling through rocky underground soil.
To navigate backward through pitch-dark tunnels just as fast as it moves forward, the pocket gopher uses its nearly hairless, touch-sensitive tail like a blind person's cane.

After the 1980 eruption of Mount St. Helens, researchers airlifted pocket gophers onto the barren pumice slopes for just one day, and their digging churned up buried soil spores that jump-started plant recovery.
Fossa: Despite looking like a cross between a sleek cougar and a dachshund, the fossa is neither cat nor dog, but a giant, specialized cousin of the mongoose.

Female fossas go through a unique phase as juveniles called 'transient masculinization,' temporarily developing male-like physical traits and secreting an orange, musky chest substance until they mature.
During mating season, a female fossa claims a high branch in a single 'mating tree' for up to a week, often returning to the exact same branch year after year while males compete below.
Equipped with flexible ankles that rotate backward and a tail nearly as long as a fossa's body, the fossa is the only predator capable of chasing lemurs at full speed through the treetops.
Fossa pups are born blind and toothless, and do not leave their hidden den until they are over four months old.
Alpine marmot: Alpine marmots hibernate in tightly huddled family piles of up to 20 individuals for up to eight months a year, dropping their heartbeats to just three to five beats per minute.
During communal hibernation, older alpine marmot brothers and parents literally sacrifice their own fat reserves by periodically warming up to keep the youngest pups from freezing to death.
Alpine marmots' winter burrows are sealed from the inside with a plug of mixed grass, earth, and dung that can be several feet thick to lock out freezing alpine air.
Before diving underground for the winter, an alpine marmot purges its digestive tract completely and shrinks its stomach and intestines by roughly half.
Lookout alpine marmots emit piercing, bird-like whistles that vary in pitch and cadence depending on whether danger is approaching from the sky, like a golden eagle, or across the rocks, like a fox.
Fur seal: A fur seal's coat is so astonishingly dense, packing up to 300,000 hairs into a single square inch, that cold seawater never actually touches its skin when it dives.
Unlike true seals that wriggle on bellies, fur seals have rotating hip bones and long flippers that let them gallop across rocky beaches as fast as a running human.

While sleeping at sea, northern fur seals float on their sides in a posture called the 'jug handle,' holding one front flipper tucked neatly into their hind flippers above the waves to conserve body heat.
Mother fur seals returning from week-long fishing trips can locate their single pup among thousands of noisy youngsters on a crowded rookery solely by the unique voice and scent of their baby.
When sleeping in the open ocean, a fur seal can engage unihemispheric slow-wave sleep, keeping half of its brain awake and one eye open looking into the water to watch for sharks and orcas.
Eland: Despite weighing as much as a small car, an adult male eland can leap straight over a six-foot-high fence from a standstill.
As bull elands walk, their knees make a loud, rhythmic clicking sound audible from a hundred yards away, which broadcasts their exact size and strength to rivals without a fight.
Milk from female elands contains roughly three times the butterfat and double the protein of domestic cow's milk, and resists spoiling in hot temperatures for much longer.

To survive scorching droughts without drinking water, an eland allows its core body temperature to rise by up to seven degrees Celsius during the day and releases the stored heat into the cool night air.
Both male and female elands sport tightly spiraled horns that they use like garden hooks to twist and snap high tree branches down to mouth level for the rest of the herd.
Fallow deer: Rather than growing pointed tines like most deer, mature male fallow deer grow wide, flattened, shovel-shaped antlers called 'palms.'
During the autumn rut, fallow deer bucks develop a massively enlarged Adam's apple and vocal tract, allowing them to emit deep, rhythmic, pig-like groans up to 3,000 times an hour.
When startled, fallow deer perform a stiff-legged bouncing gait called 'pronking' or 'stotting,' springing into the air with all four hooves leaving and hitting the ground simultaneously.
Ancient Romans and later Normans loved fallow deer so much as status symbols and game animals that they transported them by boat from the eastern Mediterranean across Europe and Britain.
A single herd of fallow deer can display four completely different coat colors at once: classic white-spotted chestnut, dark chocolate-black, pale sandy menil, and ghostly pure white.
Bumblebee bat: Also known as Kitti's hog-nosed bat, the bumblebee bat holds the title for the smallest skull of any mammal on Earth, with a body no bigger than a human thumb and a weight lighter than a single U.S. penny.
A bumblebee bat's upturned, pig-like snout and lack of a true tail membrane help it hover like a hummingbird while plucking tiny spiders directly off limestone cave ceilings.
Every evening, minuscule bumblebee bats limit their hunting trips to just 30 minutes at dusk and 20 minutes at dawn, spending the rest of their lives roosting deep inside limestone caverns.
Even though bumblebee bats roost in large caves, individuals never huddle together in clusters like other bats, preferring to hang spaced evenly apart along the rock walls.
Because a bumblebee bat's wings flap so rapidly and silently, local villagers along Thailand's Kwai River knew them simply as 'flying bumblebees' until scientists formally described them in 1974.
Patagonian mara: Looking like a jackrabbit on the front half and a miniature deer on the back half, the Patagonian mara is actually a giant rodent closely related to the household guinea pig.
Patagonian maras form strictly monogamous pairs for life, with the male constantly shadowing his mate and marking the ground around her to ward off bachelor rivals.
Even though Patagonian mara pairs stay fiercely loyal to each other in the open, up to 20 different couples will share a single communal underground nursery burrow for their pups.
A Patagonian mara mother never enters the communal nursery burrow; instead, she sits outside and calls out until only her own biological pups run out to nurse, briskly chasing away any freeloaders.
When fleeing across windswept scrublands, a Patagonian mara can switch between a rabbit-like hop, a horse-like gallop, and a four-footed spring called stotting at speeds up to 28 miles per hour.
Crested porcupine: Before launching an attack, a crested porcupine shakes a group of hollow, open-ended quills on its short tail that rattle together like a maraca to warn predators away.
Despite the enduring cartoon myth, crested porcupines cannot shoot their quills; instead, they charge backward or sideways at high speed to slam their barbed spines into an attacker's face.

Each detached crested porcupine quill is coated in natural fatty acids that act as a mild antibiotic, evolved not to help predators, but so the porcupine doesn't get fatal infections when it accidentally pokes itself falling out of rocks.
Crested porcupines are obsessive bone collectors, dragging sun-bleached skeletons, antlers, and even ivory tusks back to their underground burrows to gnaw on for calcium and to sharpen their teeth.
A crested porcupine's quills are modified hairs filled with a spongy, foam-like core that makes them buoyant enough to help the porcupine float effortlessly when swimming.
Dik-dik: The dik-dik is a miniature antelope that gets its name from the high-pitched 'zik-zik' or 'dik-dik' alarm whistle that females blow through their noses when running in a zigzag pattern from predators.
When overheated, a dik-dik elongates its flexible nose and pants rapidly to cool venous blood inside its nasal passages before that blood circulates to its brain.
Monogamous dik-dik pairs mark the borders of their territory by poking twigs directly into a dark, sticky tear-like paste secreted from large pits right below the inside corners of their eyes.
Even at full adult size, a dik-dik stands barely 12 to 16 inches tall at the shoulder and can easily hide behind a single clump of tall grass.
Look closely at a male dik-dik's forehead and you'll often see his spiky horns almost completely swallowed by an unruly tuft of fluffy crown hair.
Raccoon dog: Despite looking almost identical to a North American raccoon, complete with a bandit mask, the raccoon dog is a true wild canid most closely related to foxes.
The raccoon dog is the only member of the entire dog family (Canidae) on Earth that truly hibernates during the harsh winter months, packing on up to 50 percent more body weight in autumn.
Unlike almost all other dogs, the raccoon dog has curved claws and short legs adapted for climbing straight up tree trunks to forage for persimmons, berries, and bird eggs.
Raccoon dogs do not bark like domestic dogs; instead, they communicate with high-pitched whines, growls, and a soft, cat-like mewing sound.
In Japanese folklore, the raccoon dog is celebrated as the tanuki, a cheerful, shape-shifting trickster spirit famous for using magic leaves to disguise itself and drumming on its own belly.
River otter: River otters are famous for building slick 'slides' on mudbanks and snowdrifts, plunging down on their bellies repeatedly not just to travel fast, but purely for play.
To stay dry in icy rivers, a river otter constantly rubs and rolls on grassy banks to work natural oils from its skin into a double coat so thick that air bubbles get trapped like a wetsuit.
The long, stiff whiskers (vibrissae) on a river otter's muzzle are so sensitive to underwater vibrations that it can track the wake of a darting fish in pitch-black, muddy water.
When a river otter dives, its nostrils and ears automatically snap shut with watertight muscular valves, and its heart rate slows down to stretch its oxygen supply.
River otters create communal bathroom spots along shorelines called 'sprainting sites,' where they perform an energetic, tail-lifting 'poop dance' to leave scent messages for neighbors.
Gray squirrel: Gray squirrels are unwitting forest builders: because they bury thousands of individual nuts every autumn using spatial memory and forget roughly a quarter of them, they plant countless oak trees.

When a gray squirrel suspects another squirrel or a blue jay is watching, it performs 'deceptive caching', digging a hole, pretending to pat a nut inside with its nose, and covering the empty hole while hiding the real nut in its mouth.
When descending a tree trunk headfirst, a gray squirrel rotates its hind ankles a full 180 degrees so its rear claws point backward and hook securely into the bark like crampons.

The gray squirrel's Latin species name carolinensis sits alongside Sciurus, which comes from ancient Greek words meaning 'shadow-tail,' a nod to the way squirrels hold their bushy tails over their backs like a parasol.
A gray squirrel uses its tail as a built-in thermostat, twitching it and pumping hot blood into it on sweltering days, or wrapping it tightly around its nose in blizzards.
North Pacific right whale: In the 19th century, commercial whalers named North Pacific right whales 'right whales' because they swam slowly near shore, yielded massive amounts of oil and baleen, and conveniently floated rather than sinking when killed.

Recently, bioacousticians discovered that eastern North Pacific right whales sing complex, patterned songs featuring repeating rhythms of 'gunshot' sounds and low moans; the first time singing was ever recorded in a right whale species.

Each North Pacific right whale has a unique constellation of rough, calcified skin patches on its head called callosities, which appear white not because of the skin itself, but because millions of tiny whale lice live on them.
A North Pacific right whale's arched upper jaw holds up to 250 plates of feathery baleen per side, each growing over eight feet long to strain microscopic copepods from the water.
Because North Pacific right whales have heads that make up nearly a third of their total body length and lack a dorsal fin on their wide backs, they can push right through thin sea ice to breathe.
Goa: The goa gets its scientific name, picticaudata ('painted tail'), from the crisp, heart-shaped white patch on its rump that flashes brightly when it sprints across the high plateau.
Living comfortably at altitudes up to 18,000 feet where oxygen is half that of sea level, the goa has a remarkably oversized heart and extra-dense red blood cells.
Instead of barking or bleating loudly when a wolf approaches, a goa relies almost entirely on ultrasonic-like silent visual flashes of its white rump patch and short nasal snorts.
Only male goas carry horns, which curve gracefully backward like slender black scimitars with finely ridged rings along their length.
During the dead of winter when temperatures plummet below minus 30 degrees Fahrenheit, the goa's hollow guard hairs trap warm air around its skin like thousands of miniature thermoses.
Southern right whale: Southern right whales practice a remarkable behavior called 'sailing,' sticking their massive tail flukes straight up into the air to catch the wind and glide effortlessly across the water's surface.

Male southern right whales do not fight brutally with teeth or horns for mates; instead, they compete via 'sperm competition,' possessing the largest testes of any animal on Earth, weighing nearly a ton per pair.
A southern right whale has two widely separated blowholes instead of a single spout, shooting out two distinct plumes of mist in a signature V-shape up to 16 feet high.
Curious southern right whales along the coast of Argentina frequently swim right up to beaches and gently poke surfers, kayaks, and paddleboards with their rostrums.
Around five percent of southern right whale calves are born almost completely white, a condition called grey-morphism, before gradually darkening into a slate-grey or black coat as they grow up.
North Atlantic right whale: Before a female North Atlantic right whale chooses a mate, she often rolls onto her back at the surface to keep her belly out of reach while up to 30 suitors jostle around her in a frothy 'surface active group.'

When North Atlantic right whale mothers and newborn calves travel through busy waters, they switch to 'acoustic crypsis,' dropping their calls to whisper-quiet grunts barely louder than the crashing waves so killer whales cannot eavesdrop.

Scientists have tracked individual North Atlantic right whales for over 40 years using aerial photographs of the distinctive white callosity patches on their heads, which remain unchanged like fingerprints for life.
To feed, a North Atlantic right whale swims open-mouthed through dense underwater clouds of rice-sized copepods, filtering thousands of gallons of water per minute through its frayed baleen.
Because a North Atlantic right whale's blubber layer can be well over a foot thick, the whale struggles to shed excess body heat if it swims into warm tropical waters.
Red wolf: Red wolves are so secretive and nocturnal that biologists tracking them with radio collars have walked within yards of a resting pack in dense brush without ever seeing or hearing a single wolf.

When greeting packmates or alerting the family to intruders, red wolves communicate with a rich repertoire of body language and a unique vocalization that blends a wolf howl with a high-pitched coyote yip.
Both red wolf parents, along with older brothers and sisters from previous years' litters, take turns regurgitating food for new pups and babysitting them while the rest of the pack hunts.
During the warmer summer months, a red wolf sheds its thick winter coat to reveal oversized, radar-like ears that help dissipate body heat and pinpoint rustling rodents in tall marsh grass.

After being declared extinct in the wild in 1980 after the last survivors were brought into captivity, the red wolf became the first large carnivore ever reintroduced from a captive-breeding program into its native landscape.
Hartebeest: The hartebeest's name comes from the Dutch settlers' word hertebeest ('stag-ox'), inspired by its long, narrow face and bizarrely twisted horns that rise from a single bony pedestal on top of its skull.
Because a hartebeest's eyes sit so high up at the very top of its elongated skull, it can graze with its nose buried deep in tall savanna grass while still scanning the horizon for lions.
Rather than hiding when a predator is spotted, a sentinel hartebeest often climbs on top of a tall termite mound to stand like a statue and keep watch over the herd.

When a hartebeest calf is born, its sandy coat matches the dry grass so closely that its mother leaves it hidden alone in the brush for weeks, visiting only briefly to nurse so her scent doesn't give its spot away.
Although hartebeests look stiff and awkward with their steeply sloping backs, they can bolt at 45 miles per hour and weave through acacia scrub with sudden sideways dodges.
Sumatran rhinoceros: Covered in patches of coarse, reddish-brown bristles, especially when young, the Sumatran rhinoceros is known as the 'hairy rhino' and is the closest living relative to the extinct Ice Age woolly rhinoceros.

Unlike quieter rhinoceros species, the Sumatran rhinoceros is extraordinarily vocal, constantly conversing through the rainforest with melodic 'eeps,' whale-like whistles, and low, humming 'whale-blows.'

As the smallest of all living rhinos, the Sumatran rhinoceros spends hours every day wallowing in deep mud pits; if deprived of mud, its surprisingly sensitive skin quickly cracks and becomes inflamed.
Using a hooked upper lip and stubby horns, a Sumatran rhinoceros pushes over saplings up to three inches thick just to munch on the tender leaves at the crown.
Sumatran rhinoceroses are skilled mountain climbers that carve well-worn, tunnel-like highways through dense bamboo and thorny vines up steep volcanic ridges.
Marsh rice rat: Unlike almost all other rats, the marsh rice rat is semi-aquatic and can dive underwater and swim over 30 feet beneath the surface in a single breath to escape hawks and owls.
A marsh rice rat's dense coat traps a shimmering silver layer of microscopic air bubbles underwater, keeping the rat warm and naturally buoyant even in chilly tidal marshes.
During high tides that flood the salt marshes, the marsh rice rat weaves a waterproof, grapefruit-sized ball of cordgrass suspended high in the reeds, complete with a hidden bottom entrance.
Rather than sticking to seeds and plants, the marsh rice rat is an aggressive nocturnal hunter that raids fiddler crab burrows, cracks open marsh snails, and even snatches baby marsh wrens.
On the Florida Keys, isolated populations of marsh rice rats evolved a unique silver coat color, earning them the nickname 'silver rice rat.'
Sei whale: The sei whale is one of the fastest cetaceans in the ocean, capable of surging through the water at bursts of over 30 miles per hour.

Unlike other baleen whales that either gulp huge mouthfuls of water or skim the surface, the sei whale is a versatile 'switch-hitter' that can do both depending on whether it's chasing fish or copepods.

Rather than arching a sei whale's back and lifting its tail flukes high into the air when diving like a humpback, a sei whale simply sinks straight beneath the waves, leaving behind a series of swirling 'fluke prints' on the glassy surface.
The sei whale's name comes from the Norwegian word for pollock (seje), because the whales used to arrive off the coast of Norway at the exact same time each year as massive schools of those fish.
A sei whale's baleen plates are uniquely fringed with ultra-fine, silky white hairs that look and feel remarkably like sheep's wool.
Nilgai: Despite the nilgai's popular nickname 'blue bull,' it is not a bull at all, but a massive antelope with a striking slate-blue coat in adult males and a sandy-brown coat in females.
In India, the nilgai's name literally translates to 'blue cow,' which for centuries granted it cultural protection among Hindus who associated it with sacred cattle.
To reach high acacia leaves and blossoms, a heavy nilgai can rear up and balance stably on its hind legs like a goat.

An entire herd of nilgai uses the exact same communal dung pile day after day, sometimes building a mound up to ten feet wide, which serves as a neighborhood bulletin board and reduces parasite spread across pastures.
Unlike long-horned antelopes such as the eland and kudu, male nilgai sport short, lethal, dagger-sharp conical horns and fight rivals by dropping to their front knees and wrestling neck-to-neck.
Banteng: Adult male bantengs develop a thick, hairless, horny shield of skin across their forehead between their horns that acts as a helmet during head-butting matches.
Banteng calves and females are a bright chestnut-red, while mature bulls undergo a dramatic color change, turning dark bluish-black or chocolate brown as they age.
All bantengs sport immaculate white 'stockings' on their lower legs and a stark white rump patch that flashes like a beacon when the herd flees into dark forest cover.
A domesticated form of the banteng known as Bali cattle has been used as a draft animal in Indonesia for centuries and makes up roughly a quarter of the country's cattle population.
In 2003, scientists successfully cloned a wild banteng from frozen skin cells saved at the San Diego Zoo, using a domestic beef cow as the surrogate mother.
Baiji: Known in Chinese folklore as the 'Goddess of the Yangtze,' legend held that the baiji was the reincarnation of a princess who leaped into the river to escape a greedy stepfather.
Because the muddy waters of the Yangtze River made vision nearly useless, the baiji's eyes were reduced to tiny, pinhole-sized organs placed high on its head.
A resident male baiji named Qiqi lived in a Wuhan dolphinarium for over 22 years, providing nearly everything scientists ever learned about the species' acoustics and physiology.
Unlike oceanic dolphins that travel in large, noisy pods, the baiji had an unusually quiet echolocation click and rested for hours in calm eddy currents behind sandbars.
A baiji's long, narrow beak curved slightly upward at the tip like a pair of tweezers, allowing it to probe muddy river bottoms for bottom-dwelling catfish.
Gray mouse lemur: The gray mouse lemur, despite being a primate, sings ultrasonic courtship songs completely above the range of human hearing, punctuated by high-pitched whistles.
Before the dry season begins, the gray mouse lemur binges on sugary insect secretions and stores almost all the excess fat inside its tail, which swells up like a plump sausage.
A gray mouse lemur's brain weighs less than two grams, making it the smallest brain of any known primate, yet the lemur excels at complex spatial memory tests to relocate fruiting trees.
The gray mouse lemur survives chilly, food-scarce winters by entering daily torpor or even weeks-long hibernation inside tree hollows, dropping its body temperature to match the outside air.
During the brief breeding window, a male gray mouse lemur's testes swell to roughly 5% of his entire body weight to outcompete rivals in sperm competition.
Striped polecat: Also called the zorilla, the striped polecat has anal glands that spray a foul-smelling liquid that not only reeks like a skunk's but causes temporary blindness and a fierce burning sensation if it hits an attacker's eyes.
Before a striped polecat fires its chemical weapon, it performs a dramatic warning handstand, fluffing its long tail hair and arching its back to display its high-contrast black-and-white stripes.
If a striped polecat is cornered by a pack of predators after exhausting its spray, it can play dead so convincingly that lions and hyenas will sniff the limp body and walk away.
The striped polecat is remarkably immune to snake venom and will happily hunt puff adders and spitting cobras, dodging strikes with lightning-fast footwork.
Poor swimmers that avoid deep water, striped polecats have occasionally been observed paddling awkwardly across small streams with their bushy tails held high to stay dry.
Vaquita: The vaquita's Spanish name translates to 'little cow,' while dark rings around its eyes and curved black lip patches give it the permanent appearance of wearing mascara and smiling.
Unlike almost any other marine cetacean, the vaquita thrives in shallow, sun-baked lagoon waters where temperatures swing wildly from 14°C in winter to 36°C in summer.
A vaquita's dorsal fin is proportionally taller and wider than those of other porpoises, acting as a biological radiator to dump excess body heat in warm coastal shallows.
Wait times between vaquita sightings are so long because it surfaces with an almost imperceptible, slow forward roll that barely disturbs the water's surface and produces no visible blow.
Western science had no idea the vaquita existed until 1958, when three weather-bleached skulls washed up on a beach in Baja California.
Lamia: Rather than curling downward like a monkey's tail, the tip of a lamia's prehensile tail is hairless and grips branches by wrapping upward over the top.
The scales along a lamia's tail aren't arranged in neat rings like a sewer rat's, but overlap like roof shingles in spiral rows with three tiny hairs poking out from under each scale.
Instead of excavating dirt burrows, the lamia chews circular entrance holes into hollow tree limbs and weaves cozy spherical nests out of shredded palm fibers.
A lamia's skull has a noticeably domed, broad forehead and heavy brow ridges that give its face a surprisingly blunt, pug-like profile compared to typical field mice.
Female lamias have only four nipples located near the groin, and their nursing pups cling so tightly to them that the mother can drag the entire litter along if startled from her nest.
Wildcat: Unlike domestic tabbies whose tails taper to a sharp point, the wildcat sports a thick, blunt-ended tail banded with black rings that looks like a furry club.
Even when hand-raised from birth with bottle-feeding and constant affection, wildcat kittens retain a fierce, untamable streak and will hiss and spit at humans as adults.
A Near Eastern wildcat buried alongside a human on the island of Cyprus 9,500 years ago provided the earliest archaeological evidence of cats living beside people.

In the Scottish Highlands, centuries of interbreeding between wildcats and feral domestic cats have created a 'hybrid swarm' so extensive that genetically pure individuals are nearly impossible to find in the wild.
The soles of a wildcat's paws are jet-black and heavily furred between the pads to muffle footsteps when stalking rodents across crisp winter snow or dry leaves.
European polecat: Around 2,500 years ago, people bred and domesticated the feisty European polecat to create the modern pet ferret, originally used to flush rabbits out of underground warrens.

When a European polecat catches more frogs and toads than it can eat in autumn, it bites them at the base of the skull to paralyze them without killing them, keeping fresh live rations stacked in its burrow all winter.
The European polecat, unlike solitary stoats or weasels, has a remarkably low metabolic rate for a mustelid and can survive weeks of bitter frost curled tightly inside an abandoned rabbit hole.
In medieval England, the European polecat's habit of raiding henhouses earned it the Old French nickname 'poul-chat' (chicken-cat), which gradually morphed into its modern English name.
A European polecat neutralizes the poisonous skin secretions of common toads by frantically rolling the amphibian through damp grass and soil like a baker kneading dough before taking a bite.
Rice's whale: For decades Rice's whale was mistaken for a local subpopulation of another whale until a skull washed into the Everglades in 2019, revealing unique bone structures around the blowhole that proved it was an entirely distinct species.
Unlike almost all other baleen whales that embark on epic pole-to-equator migrations, Rice's whale spends its entire life year-round in a single narrow depth belt in the northeastern Gulf of Mexico.
During the day Rice's whale dives deeply to hover just above the sea floor at 200 meters to gulp schools of lanternfish, then spends nearly 90% of the night resting within 15 meters of the surface.
Instead of displaying three symmetrical ridges along the top of a Rice's whale's snout like its closest relatives, its lateral ridges are tucked inside shallow grooves.
A Rice's whale's low-frequency moans include a distinctive 'long-moan' call lasting over twenty seconds that pulses like a slow heartbeat through the deep gulf waters.
Indiana bat: True to the Indiana bat's name, the first specimen ever described by science was discovered inside Wyandotte Cave in southern Indiana in 1904, where millions once wintered.
During winter hibernation, Indiana bats pack onto cave ceilings so tightly, up to 4,800 individuals per square meter, that the rock surface looks like a single thick pelt of brown fur.
Female Indiana bats mate in autumn before hibernating, store the live sperm inside their reproductive tracts all winter long, and only fertilize the egg once they wake up in spring.
In summer, up to a hundred pregnant female Indiana bats squeeze underneath the peeling, sun-warmed bark of dead shagbark hickory trees, which act as natural solar incubators for their pups.
A single nursing female Indiana bat can catch and devour up to half her own body weight in moths, caddisflies, and beetles in a single night.
Blackbuck: A male blackbuck's horns twist in tight corkscrew spirals up to four full turns and are ringed with prominent ridges from base to tip.
Once monsoon season ends, dominant male blackbucks can change coat color back and forth, fading from jet-black to light tan when hormone levels drop, then darkening again before the next rut.
When startled on open plains, an entire blackbuck herd erupts into 'pronking', leaping two meters straight into the air with stiff legs before breaking into an 80-kilometer-per-hour sprint.

During courtship displays, a male blackbuck tilts his nose straight up toward the sky, lays his long spiral horns flat along his back, and struts with short, mincing steps while flipping his white tail.
Under Emperor Akbar in 16th-century Mughal India, royal trainers kept stables of tame cheetahs specifically to course fleet-footed blackbucks across the plains.
Alcathoe whiskered bat: The Alcathoe whiskered bat is named after Alcathoe, a princess in Greek mythology whom Dionysus transformed into a bat for refusing to join his revels and choosing to weave indoors instead.

The Alcathoe whiskered bat went completely unrecognized by science until 2001 because it looks almost identical to two cousin species, until researchers noticed its echolocation clicks pitched up to a sizzling 120 kilohertz.
As Europe's smallest whiskered bat, the Alcathoe whiskered bat weighs roughly the same as a single penny (about 3.5 to 5 grams) and can comfortably curl up inside a walnut shell.
Instead of roosting in caves or church attics like many bats, the Alcathoe whiskered bat prefers tiny lightning cracks and woodpecker holes high in the canopy of old-growth oak and sycamore trees.
You can tell an adult Alcathoe whiskered bat apart from its lookalike cousins by its pinkish-brown snout, short ears with a notch on the outer edge, and miniature feet.
African forest elephant: Unlike its savanna cousin, which has four toenails on the front foot and three on the back, the African forest elephant has five rounded toenails on the front and four on the back.
An African forest elephant's tusks don't curve outward and upward, but grow straight down toward the ground so they won't snag on thick jungle vines as it pushes through dense undergrowth.
The ivory of an African forest elephant's tusks has a subtle pinkish tint and is much harder and denser than savanna ivory, helping it crack open rock-hard seeds of forest trees like Panda oleosa.

So many rain forest tree species rely exclusively on the African forest elephant to swallow their seeds and deposit them miles away in nutrient-rich dung piles that botanists call them 'megagardener' trees.
Groups of African forest elephants gather in muddy forest clearings called bais, where they kneel down to dig up mineral-rich clay and socialize through ground-shaking, infrasonic rumbles.
Irrawaddy dolphin: Completely lacking a sleek dolphin beak, the Irrawaddy dolphin has a high, rounded forehead and highly mobile lips that allow it to make comical, expressive faces underwater.
An Irrawaddy dolphin can spit cohesive jets of water up to 1.5 meters into the air from its mouth, a trick it uses both during social play and to herd panicked schools of fish into tight balls.

Along the Ayeyarwady River in Myanmar, wild Irrawaddy dolphin pods cooperate with traditional fishermen, slapping their flukes to signal when fish are near the boat and driving the catch directly into cast nets.
Unlike almost all other dolphins, an Irrawaddy dolphin's neck vertebrae are not fused together, allowing it to turn its head side-to-side and nod like a human.
Despite living in muddy freshwater rivers a thousand kilometers inland, DNA reveals the Irrawaddy dolphin's closest living relative is actually the killer whale.
Gaur: Standing up to 2.2 meters at the shoulder and weighing well over a metric ton, the gaur is the heaviest and most muscular wild bovine on Earth.
Adult gaur bulls secrete an oily, aromatic sweat called 'seladang oil' that gives their dark coats a musky scent and is believed to act as a natural insect repellent in steamy jungles.
Rather than charging straight into an opponent head-on, rival gaur bulls circle each other sideways with their heads lowered to show off the towering muscular ridge along their shoulders.
A gaur's massive, upward-curving horns grow from a bulging pale-yellow boss across the forehead and are always tipped with glossy black points.
Tigers are the only predators bold enough to ambush an adult gaur, and even then, a herd will sometimes form a defensive phalanx and trample a stalking big cat to death.
Silky sifaka: Nicknamed the 'angel of the forest' for its long, snow-white fur, the silky sifaka is one of the rarest primates on Earth and has never survived for long in captivity outside its native rainforest.
Although a silky sifaka's coat is pure white, the skin on its face, ears, and palms starts out jet-black in youth and gradually loses pigment with age, turning mottled pink in older adults.
Male silky sifakas use a dark, bare scent gland right in the center of their chest to rub a pungent musky mark onto tree trunks, often gouging the bark with their teeth first.
The silky sifaka moves through the canopy by vertical clinging and leaping, launching itself sideways across 10-meter gaps between vertical trunks without ever touching the ground.
Even newborn silky sifaka infants have a shockingly strong grip, locking their fingers into the long silky fur on their mother's belly while she bounds effortlessly through the treetops.
Cotton-top tamarin: A cotton-top tamarin's wild shock of flowing white hair puffs straight up like a punk-rock mohawk whenever it is startled or angry, making its tiny head look twice its actual size.
Cotton-top tamarin fathers and older brothers do almost all the heavy lifting of childcare, carrying twin babies on their backs all day and only handing them back to the mother to nurse.
While carrying heavy infants, caring cotton-top tamarin fathers actually lose up to 10% of their body weight due to the energy spent hauling the twins through the branches and sharing food with them.
A cotton-top tamarin's vocal repertoire of 38 distinct chirps, whistles, and trills is arranged using syntax-like rules, combining warning calls with food calls in specific sequences.
Within a cotton-top tamarin family troop, only the dominant female ovulates; she releases pheromones in her scent marks that chemically suppress pregnancy in all her subordinate daughters.
Ethiopian wolf: Despite its name and coyote-like build, the Ethiopian wolf ignores large hoofed prey and is a specialist rodent hunter, subsisting almost entirely on giant mole-rats and grass rats.

Researchers stunned the scientific world by photographing Ethiopian wolves lapping sugary nectar from red-hot poker flowers, dusting their muzzles in yellow pollen and acting as the first known large carnivore pollinators.
To catch a giant mole-rat weighing nearly two pounds, an Ethiopian wolf stalks in slow motion around a burrow entrance and waits motionless for up to an hour before lunging face-first into the dirt.

Rather than avoiding local herds of gelada monkeys, the Ethiopian wolf calmly walks right through the middle of grazing troops, using the monkeys as living camouflage so nearby rodents don't spot the wolf approaching.
Ethiopian wolf packs patrol freezing Afro-alpine plateaus above 4,000 meters in elevation, greeting each other at dawn and dusk with high-pitched, chorus-like yips and howls.
Diademed sifaka: Named for the bright crown-like ring of white fur framing a diademed sifaka's black face, its hindquarters and legs glow in brilliant shades of golden-orange and silver-gray.
To fuel a diademed sifaka's explosive leaps between tree trunks, it seeks out high-energy seeds and parasitic mistletoe flowers, trekking over a mile each day through steep cloud forests.
Female diademed sifakas sit firmly at the top of the troop's social ladder, getting first pick of the ripest fruit and cuffing adult males on the nose if they try to eat out of turn.

A diademed sifaka's alarm call for aerial predators like the Madagascar harrier-hawk is a roaring bark, whereas ground predators trigger a sneezing sound that sounds distinctly like 'tzisk-tzisk-tzisk'; the origin of the word sifaka.

Because a diademed sifaka's hind legs are so much longer than its arms, if forced onto flat ground it cannot walk on all fours, instead hopping sideways like a miniature ballet dancer with its arms held overhead.
Grey seal: The grey seal's Latin name, Halichoerus grypus, translates directly to 'hook-nosed sea-pig', a nod to the adult bull's huge, arched Roman nose and noisy snorting.
Grey seal bulls communicate territory boundaries underwater without opening their mouths by clapping their front flippers together so forcefully that the crack sounds like a gunshot.
Grey seal pups are born wrapped in creamy white lanugo fur and drink milk that is nearly 60% pure fat, allowing them to gain over three pounds of blubber every single day.

After only three weeks of nursing, a grey seal mother abruptly abandons her beachball-round pup on the shore, where the youngster fasts for up to a month while molting its baby coat before ever touching the ocean.
In Celtic folklore throughout Orkney and the Hebrides, the soulful, human-like eyes of grey seals inspired legends of the Selkies; magical beings who shed their seal skins to walk on land as humans.
Saola: Often called the 'Asian Unicorn,' the saola remained completely unknown to science until 1992, when surveyors found a pair of strange, spindle-horned skulls hanging in a hunter's house in Vietnam.
A saola's face is dotted with remarkably huge scent glands along the muzzle that are covered by movable fleshy flaps; when lifted, they secrete a thick greenish-white paste used to mark rocks.
Both male and female saolas carry a pair of razor-sharp, nearly straight horns up to half a meter long that slant backward at the exact same angle as a traditional Vietnamese weaving spindle.
Though the saola looks like a cross between an Arabian oryx and an antelope, DNA analyses proved it is actually a primitive relative of wild cattle and buffaloes.
No biologist has ever directly observed a saola living in the wild; every piece of footage from its mountain forest home has come from automated motion-triggered camera traps.
European hare: The famous phrase 'mad as a March hare' comes not from fighting male European hares, but from annoyed females rising onto their hind legs and boxing persistent suitors right in the nose with their front paws.

Through an extraordinary reproductive quirk called superfetation, a pregnant female European hare can conceive a brand-new second litter of embryos inside her womb before she has even given birth to the first litter.
Unlike rabbits that give birth to blind, naked kits deep underground, European hares drop their babies right in the open grass; fully furred, wide-eyed, and ready to hop within minutes of birth.
To evade greyhounds and foxes, a European hare can hit speeds of 70 kilometers per hour while executing sudden 90-degree zigzags and doubling back over its own scent trail.

A mother European hare visits her scattered leverets only once a day for less than five minutes right after sunset, nursing them with super-rich milk so her scent doesn't draw predators to their hiding spots.
Javan rhinoceros: The Javan rhinoceros's thick gray skin folds into dramatic, overlapping plates across its shoulders, back, and rump, giving it the unmistakable look of wearing medieval plate armor.

Unlike African rhinos that carry two formidable horns, only male Javan rhinoceroses grow a single modest horn, usually shorter than 20 centimeters, while females often have only a small bump or no horn at all.
Instead of using its horn to fight predators or rivals, the Javan rhinoceros uses it primarily to scrape mud in wallows and pull down high saplings so its prehensile upper lip can strip the leaves.

Once found from eastern India all the way across Southeast Asia, the entire global population of Javan rhinoceroses now lives inside a single peninsula at Ujung Kulon National Park on the western tip of Java.
Because the Javan rhinoceros spends hours soaking in deep mud holes to prevent sunburn and biting flies, its skin often dries with a reddish or blackish crust depending on the local soil.
Bryde's whale: Bryde's whale is the only baleen whale you can identify at a glance from above by the three parallel ridges running from the tip of its snout back to its blowholes.

Rather than skimming quietly through plankton, a Bryde's whale often lunges straight up out of the water with its jaws wide open, gulping a swimming-pool-sized mouthful of anchovies before clamping its baleen shut.

In the Gulf of Thailand, Bryde's whales have perfected a lazy 'tread-water' feeding technique: they poke their open jaws vertically above the waves and wait as panicked fish leap directly into their mouths to escape seabirds.
Named after Johan Bryde, the Norwegian consul who built the first modern whaling stations in South Africa in the early 1900s, the Bryde's whale's name is actually pronounced 'BROO-duhz.'
Unlike humpbacks or blues that fast for months while migrating to icy polar waters, the warm-water Bryde's whale stays in tropical and temperate seas above 16°C all year round.
Mule deer: Instead of running at a normal gallop like a white-tailed deer, the mule deer escapes up rocky canyon slopes using a four-footed bounce called 'stotting,' where all four hooves strike the ground and push off simultaneously like a pogo stick.
A mule deer's oversized ears, nearly a foot long and independent like radar dishes, inspired Lewis and Clark to give the animal its barnyard nickname during their 1804 expedition.
You can tell a mule deer's antlers apart from a white-tail's because the beams fork into two equal branches that each fork again, rather than growing single tines off one main beam.

A mule deer buck residing in southwestern Wyoming named '255' was tracked by GPS collar making the longest documented land-mammal migration in the lower 48 states: a 390-kilometer trek across mountain passes and highways twice a year.
When threatened by a coyote, a mule deer doe won't always flee; mothers frequently team up to rush the canine and pummel it with razor-sharp front hooves.
Waterbuck: Skin glands across a waterbuck's coat secrete a thick, musky oil when the animal is excited or wet, which waterproofs its hair as it wades through rivers.
A waterbuck's oily secretion smells and tastes so potent that it seeps into the meat if the animal isn't skinned carefully, earning it a reputation among even hungry lions as a last-resort meal.
One widely spread waterbuck subspecies sports a stark white ring painted squarely around its rump, looking exactly as if it had just sat down on a freshly painted white toilet seat.
According to an old East African folktale, the waterbuck got that white ring because it was the very first creature to test out the newly built ark's freshly painted latrine.
When chased by wild dogs or leopards, a waterbuck dives straight into deep crocodile-infested pools and stands submerged with only its nostrils and backward-swept horns poking above the surface.
Barbary macaque: The famous Barbary macaque troop living atop the Rock of Gibraltar is the only wild monkey population in Europe; British legend claims that if the monkeys ever leave the Rock, Britain will lose Gibraltar, prompting Winston Churchill to airlift reinforcements from Morocco during World War II.
Despite sometimes being called the 'Barbary ape,' the Barbary macaque is a true monkey whose external tail has shrunk to a barely visible, boneless vestigial nub.

Adult male Barbary macaques use babies as 'social passports', picking up an infant (even one that isn't theirs), carrying it over to a rival male, and chattering their teeth together over the baby to diffuse tension and build alliances.

Living high in the cedar forests of the Atlas Mountains, Barbary macaques grow thick winter coats and spend snowy days foraging under pine needles and huddling in tight, multi-monkey balls for warmth.
Female Barbary macaques mate with virtually every adult male in the troop during estrus, purposely obscuring paternity so that every male in the group treats all infants with protective care.
Drill: Although the drill's face is glossy jet-black rather than blue and red like its cousin the mandrill, a dominant male's chin is framed by a hot-pink lower lip and a snow-white beard.

What a dominant male drill lacks in facial color, he makes up for on his backside: his rump glows in vivid shades of violet, lilac, and magenta that brighten further the higher he climbs in the social hierarchy.
When greeting a troop member peacefully, a drill pulls the corners of its mouth back and shakes its head side-to-side in what looks exactly like a friendly human grin.
