Bolivar rice rat: Living in the super-wet Chocó and premontane rainforests from eastern Panama down through Colombia and Ecuador, the Bolivar rice rat is crowned with long, dark vibrissae (whiskers) that extend well past its shoulders.
The Bolivar rice rat's extra-long whiskers act like radar antennae in pitch-black, rain-drenched undergrowth, allowing the rat to map wet roots and mossy boulders without bumping its nose.
The Bolivar rice rat's large hind feet are uniquely elongated for wading through shallow forest streams and scrambling over slick, mud-coated fallen logs.
Rather than digging burrows that would instantly flood in tropical downpours, the Bolivar rice rat constructs tight, waterproof nests beneath tangled tree buttresses and rotting palm trunks.
By eating fallen rainforest seeds and fungi at night, the Bolivar rice rat plays a quiet role in recycling nutrients across one of the rainiest biodiversity hotspots on Earth.
Hammer-headed bat: Adult male hammer-headed bats look like flying gargoyles or winged moose: their skulls and muzzles are hugely inflated to house a gigantic larynx and resonating chambers that fill more than half their body cavity, crowding their heart, lungs, and intestines backward into their abdomen!

Twice a year along riverbank trees in Central Africa, up to 130 male hammer-headed bats gather in noisy 'lek' arenas where they flap their wings at double speed and blast a deafening, metallic 'kwoink-kwoink' honk like a chorus of car horns to attract picky females.
Nearly 80 percent of all matings at a hammer-headed bat lek are won by just the top 6 percent of males holding the prime central branches.
With a three-foot wingspan, the hammer-headed bat is the largest bat on the entire African continent, yet despite its terrifying face, it eats almost nothing but sweet figs and banana juice.
Female hammer-headed bats have normal, fox-like faces and weigh barely half as much as the giant-headed males, creating the most extreme sexual dimorphism of any bat species in the world.
Weddell seal: Living farther south than any other mammal on Earth, the Weddell seal thrives along the frozen edge of Antarctica in McMurdo Sound, barely 800 miles from the South Pole.

To keep breathing holes open through seven feet of rock-hard Antarctic fast ice, a Weddell seal opens its jaws 180 degrees wide and uses its protruding upper canines and incisors like an ice saw, rasping away at the freezing ice until its teeth wear down to stubs in old age.

Underwater, male Weddell seals sing an eerie, sci-fi repertoire of laser-like trills, whistles, and deep booming chirps so loud that explorers sleeping inside tents on top of the ice can feel the vibrations through their sleeping bags.
Before diving up to 2,000 feet deep for over an hour, a Weddell seal actually exhales most of the air from its lungs, relying instead on massive oxygen reserves stored in its spleen and muscles.
Because Weddell seals evolved on Antarctic ice sheets where polar bears and land predators have never existed, they have zero fear of walking humans on the ice.
Hoffmann's two-toed sloth: Hoffmann's two-toed sloth has the most variable body temperature of any mammal on Earth, swinging daily between 75°F and 92°F depending on whether it is raining or sunny, because it possesses less muscle mass for its size than almost any other land mammal and cannot shiver effectively.

Because a Hoffmann's two-toed sloth hangs upside down for nearly its entire life, the hair on its coat parts on its belly and grows downward toward its back so tropical torrential rain runs right off!

Inside the grooves of each Hoffmann's two-toed sloth hair grows a miniature ecosystem of symbiotic green algae (which camouflages the sloth as a clump of moss) and specialized 'sloth moths' that spend their entire lives in its fur.

A single meal of tough cecropia leaves can take up to a full month to pass through a Hoffmann's two-toed sloth's multi-chambered stomach; when full, digested leaves and waste account for up to a third of the sloth's entire body weight.
While almost every other mammal from a mouse to a giraffe has exactly seven neck vertebrae, Hoffmann's two-toed sloth breaks the rule by having only five to seven cervical vertebrae.
New Zealand long-tailed bat: Along with the lesser short-tailed bat, the walnut-sized New Zealand long-tailed bat is one of only two land mammals completely native to New Zealand; everything else on the islands before humans arrived was a bird, reptile, frog, or insect!
In 2021, the New Zealand long-tailed bat ('pekapeka-tou-roa' in Māori) caused an international stir when it won New Zealand's fiercely contested 'Bird of the Year' competition by a landslide.

Able to zip through dense kauri and beech forests at nearly 40 miles per hour, the New Zealand long-tailed bat emits echolocation clicks at such a high frequency (40 kilohertz) that it was once dubbed the 'silent shadow.'

Unlike cave-dwelling bats that stay in one cavern for decades, colonies of New Zealand long-tailed bats pack up and move to a brand-new hollow tree almost every single night to avoid building up parasites or attracting predators.

A New Zealand long-tailed bat's long tail is completely enclosed inside a wide membrane stretched between its hind legs (the uropatagium), which it curls forward in midair like a catcher's mitt to scoop up moths and mosquitoes on the wing.
Spider monkey: Why is it called a spider monkey? Because like its distant African cousin the colobus monkey, it has completely lost its external thumbs, leaving four long, curved fingers that hook over branches like a trapeze artist's hands as it swings at high speed.

A spider monkey's prehensile tail is longer than its entire body and features a naked, ridged friction pad on the underside with its own unique 'fingerprint' that can grip a branch tightly enough to support the monkey's entire weight while both hands pick fruit.
With a single swinging stride ('brachiation'), a spider monkey can clear 30 feet of open space through the rainforest canopy.

Ancient Maya and Aztec cultures revered the spider monkey as a divine patron of music, dance, and mischief; an entire day on the sacred 260-day Mesoamerican calendar ('Ozomatli' or 'B'atz'') is named after it.

Because spider monkeys' diet is nearly 90 percent ripe fruit and they live in 'fission-fusion' societies that split into small foraging parties by day and reunite at night, biologists found they have twice the brain size of leaf-eating howler monkeys of the exact same body weight.
Risso's dolphin: Born smooth and dark chocolate-brown, a Risso's dolphin accumulates so many permanent white scratch marks, from battling deep-sea squid and play-biting podmates, that old adults turn almost completely snow-white from head to tail.

Between 1888 and 1912, a legendary solitary Risso's dolphin named 'Pelorus Jack' escorted steamships through New Zealand's treacherous French Pass for 24 years, becoming the first individual marine mammal in history protected by an official national law.

Because Risso's dolphins feed almost exclusively on slippery squid and octopuses that they suck in whole, they have zero teeth in their upper jaw and only two to seven pairs of peg-like teeth at the tip of their lower jaw.
Running straight down the middle of a Risso's dolphin's bulbous, beakless forehead is a deep vertical crease, an acoustic channel thought to help focus echolocation beams toward deep-water prey.
Featuring one of the tallest dorsal fins in proportion to body length of any cetacean, Risso's dolphin pods are sometimes mistaken from a distance for juvenile killer whales.
Eastern cottontail: Before mating in spring, pairs of eastern cottontails perform an acrobatic courtship dance: one rabbit charges at the other, while the partner leaps up to 15 feet straight into the air over its mate's head before they switch roles.

A mother eastern cottontail visits her hidden grass-and-fur nest for only five minutes twice a day, at dawn and dusk, so her scent won't lead foxes, cats, or snakes to her babies; she isn't abandoning them, and her milk is so rich the kits only need two quick feedings every 24 hours!

When fleeing a dog or hawk, the eastern cottontail flashes the bright snow-white underside of its puffy tail while bounding in sharp zigzags, then suddenly tucks its tail down to hide the white beacon the instant it freezes in cover, making predators look for a white dot that just vanished.

Despite a typical wild lifespan of barely 15 months, a single female eastern cottontail can produce up to seven litters of five kits in a single breeding season, meaning one pair could theoretically have 350,000 descendants in five years if every bunny survived.
Eastern cottontails never dig their own burrows; in freezing winter storms, they simply move into abandoned groundhog holes or shelter beneath thick blackberry brambles.
Honey possum: Weighing less than a standard AA battery (about a third of an ounce), the tiny southwestern Australian honey possum holds the absolute world record for the longest sperm of any mammal; each sperm cell is over a third of a millimeter long, big enough to see with the naked eye!
The honey possum also boasts the largest testes relative to body weight of any mammal on Earth, accounting for more than 4.2 percent of the male's entire body mass.

As the only completely non-flying mammal in the world that survives exclusively on nectar and pollen, the honey possum has a long, pointed snout and a brush-tipped tongue that darts in and out of banksia flowers three times per second like a hummingbird's.
Because a honey possum never chews solid food, its cheek teeth have shrunk to tiny, useless pegs and its stomach has simplified into a two-chambered storage sac for flower nectar.
At birth, a honey possum joey weighs just 0.005 grams (one five-thousandth of an ounce), making it the smallest newborn of any mammal on the planet.
White-eared titi: Devoted white-eared titi couples are the ultimate romantics of the rainforest: whenever a mated pair sits together on a branch or sleeps at night, they entwine their long, furry tails around each other in a permanent spiral embrace.

Every morning at dawn, a mated pair of white-eared titis performs an intricate, synchronized vocal duet that echoes through the Bolivian canopy to tell neighboring couples that their territory is spoken for.

Outside of nursing, a white-eared titi father is the primary caregiver, carrying the single infant on his back for almost the entire day and handing the baby back to the mother only for milk breaks before taking it right back.
Lab studies show that if a mated white-eared titi is separated from its partner even briefly, its stress hormones skyrocket far more than if it is separated from its own offspring.

Sporty white ear tufts frame a white-eared titi's expressive reddish-brown face, and when a family group spots a tayra or ocelot below, they sway side to side while whipping their tails to confuse the predator.
Perrier's sifaka: Unlike its paler cousins, Perrier's sifaka is completely jet-black from head to toe, punctuated by startlingly bright ruby-orange eyes that stand out in the dark forest canopy.
When forced to cross open ground between trees, Perrier's sifaka cannot walk on all fours and instead bounds sideways on its hind legs with its arms held aloft like a tightrope walker.
Perrier's sifaka gets the name 'sifaka' from an onomatopoeia coined by Malagasy locals to mimic its signature alarm call, an explosive 'shif-auk!' accompanied by a sharp backward whip of the head.
During the bone-dry season when streams vanish, Perrier's sifaka rarely drinks liquid water directly, extracting nearly all its moisture by chewing succulent leaves and unripe fruit.
Because Perrier's sifaka's diet consists largely of tough, fibrous foliage, its cecum, part of the large intestine, is stretched to roughly ten times the length of its stomach to ferment leaves.
Moor macaque: When happy or trying to defuse tension with a rival, the moor macaque of Sulawesi pulls its lips back into a silent, toothy grin accompanied by rapid lip-smacking, a gesture that means friendship rather than aggression.

Living on an island free of large feline predators like tigers or leopards, the moor macaque has evolved a remarkably laid-back, egalitarian society where fights are rare and reconciliations happen within seconds.
Adult moor macaques lose the pale facial skin of their youth to become entirely charcoal-black, accented by a horseshoe-shaped pad of bare pink skin on their rumps.
Rather than hoarding food, moor macaques frequently allow younger troop members to take fig fruits directly out of their hands or mouths without protest.
A moor macaque's tail is reduced to a tiny, barely visible nub under two centimeters long, leading early European explorers to mistakenly classify it as an ape.
Kodkod: As the smallest wild cat in the Americas, a full-grown adult kodkod weighs roughly the same as a two-liter bottle of soda and has a skull smaller than a tennis ball.
Despite a kodkod's miniature frame, it possesses disproportionately wide, muscular paws with long curved claws that turn it into a vertical-climbing acrobat among bamboo thickets.
Up to a third of the kodkod population on Chiloé Island is completely melanistic, sporting a sleek black coat where faint spots are only visible when sunlight hits at an angle.
In the mythology of the indigenous Mapuche people, who call the kodkod the 'Guiña,' this nocturnal prowler was superstitiously blamed for sneaking into coops to drink chicken blood.
Unlike most cats that despise getting wet, the kodkod lives in temperate Valdivian rainforests that receive over 150 inches of rain a year and readily swims across cold mountain streams.
Takin: Legend holds that the bizarre Himalayan takin was created by the 15th-century Tibetan 'Divine Madman' Lam Drukpa Kunley, who fused the skull of a goat onto the skeleton of a cow after eating both for lunch.
A takin's thick, golden fleece inspired ancient Greek traders along the Silk Road and is thought by some historians to be the real-life inspiration behind the myth of Jason and the Golden Fleece.
Lacking normal sweat glands, a takin's skin secretes a bitter, oily red substance that coats its fur like a natural raincoat to repel freezing mountain fog and torrential monsoons.
Inside a takin's oversized, arched Roman nose are huge sinus cavities that warm frigid Himalayan air before it ever reaches the animal's lungs, preventing internal frostbite.
Despite weighing as much as a grand piano and having short, stocky legs, a takin can leap six feet straight from one jagged cliff ledge to another.
Small Indian civet: For centuries across Asia, royal apothecaries collected the pasty, musky secretion from the small Indian civet's perineal glands, known as 'civetone', to fix the scent of luxury perfumes and incense.
Even though the small Indian civet belongs to the carnivore order, it has a sweet tooth for palm sap and often raids toddy pots hung by human harvesters high in coconut trees.
A small Indian civet rarely digs its own home, frequently moving instead into abandoned termite mounds, hollow logs, or the spaces underneath village floorboards and rafters.
Along a small Indian civet's spine runs a crest of stiff hairs that stay flat when calm but flare upright like a punk-rock mohawk the instant it feels cornered.
A small Indian civet's pupils are vertical slits like a domestic cat's, paired with sensitive facial whiskers that allow it to sprint along narrow tree branches in pitch darkness.
Northern pig-tailed macaque: Named for its short, semi-erect tail that arches over its back like a piglet's, the northern pig-tailed macaque uses subtle flicks and curls of that tail to signal social rank to troop mates.
In parts of Thailand and Malaysia, coastal villagers have historically trained northern pig-tailed macaques to climb towering palms and twist off only the ripest coconuts on command.
The northern pig-tailed macaque is one of the few monkeys that deliberately raids subterranean termite nests and then rubs crushed millipedes or ants into its fur as a natural insect repellent.

To communicate through dense jungle foliage without alerting predators, northern pig-tailed macaques purse their lips forward in a silent 'pucker' expression that invites grooming or peaceful approach.

Equipped with stretchy cheek pouches as large as its actual stomach, a foraging northern pig-tailed macaque can stuff a full meal of figs into its face and sprint back to the canopy to chew in safety.
Golden angwantibo: Instead of leaping between branches like most primates, the nocturnal golden angwantibo creeps through the canopy with fluid, slow-motion precision so leaves never rustle to betray its position.

A golden angwantibo's hands are modified into living pincers: the index finger is reduced to a tiny boneless stub, widening the span between the thumb and remaining fingers for an unbreakable vise grip.
Over 80 percent of a golden angwantibo's diet consists of toxic, foul-tasting caterpillars covered in stinging spines, which the angwantibo meticulously wipes against tree bark before swallowing.
When threatened by a tree snake or eagle, a golden angwantibo tucks its head between its forelegs to expose the back of its neck, which is reinforced with raised vertebral spines and thick skin.

A network of intertwined blood vessels in a golden angwantibo's wrists and ankles, called a rete mirabile, prevents lactic acid buildup, allowing it to hang upside down by its feet for hours without cramping.
Atlantic white-sided dolphin: One of the most colorful cetaceans in the northern seas, the Atlantic white-sided dolphin sports a distinctive tri-tone flank with a bright white patch stacked directly above a streak of golden-yellow ochre.

Rather than the dramatic vertical leaps of bottlenose dolphins, the Atlantic white-sided dolphin prefers high-speed 'charging' at the water's surface, kicking up a rooster-tail of spray as it slices through swells.
Pods of Atlantic white-sided dolphins have been documented babysitting and swimming alongside stranded or solitary pilot whales and fin whales for days at a time.
Each newborn Atlantic white-sided dolphin calf arrives in the world with a row of tiny whiskers along its snout that fall out shortly after birth, leaving behind microscopic sensory pits.

By examining the growth rings inside an Atlantic white-sided dolphin's conical teeth, much like counting rings on a felled oak, marine biologists have discovered that males and females form separate bachelor and maternity herds.
White-faced spiny tree-rat: Despite a humble name, the nocturnal Amazonian white-faced spiny tree-rat wears a dramatic tuxedo mask of stark snowy-white fur across its nose, cheeks, and forehead.
A white-faced spiny tree-rat's back and flanks are armored with flattened, grooved spines mixed into its coat that click and rattle softly when the animal shakes itself in the canopy.
Living thirty to ninety feet above the forest floor, the white-faced spiny tree-rat rarely touches the ground in its entire life, using wide, padded hind feet to grip slick liana vines.

To crack through the rock-hard shells of unripe rainforest seeds, a white-faced spiny tree-rat's orange incisors are reinforced with iron-rich enamel that continuously sharpens itself with every bite.
When startled in a hollow-tree nest, a white-faced spiny tree-rat thumps its heavy hind feet against the resonant wood like a drum to warn family members of approaching danger.
Tayra: The tayra, a sleek, long-bodied cousin of the wolverine, is one of the only mammals outside of humans known to practice 'external ripening', picking green, inedible plantains, hiding them in a cache, and returning days later once they turn sweet.
When scanning for prey in tall grass, a tayra rises up onto its hind legs like a giant three-foot-long meerkat, weaving its head side to side to catch scents on the breeze.
Although most tayras have dark chocolate fur with a creamy throat patch, a striking blond morph found in the Guiana Shield looks as if it has been bleached by the sun.
With partially webbed toes and a long, muscular tail that acts as both a balancing pole in treetops and a rudder in rivers, a tayra can chase down squirrels in the canopy or fish in streams.
Rather than stalking silently like a cat, a hunting tayra often bounds noisily through the underbrush to flush terrified rodents and iguanas straight into its path.
Perrin's beaked whale: Perrin's beaked whale is so elusive that when four stranded specimens washed ashore in California between 1975 and 1997, scientists mistook them for Hector's beaked whales for over twenty years until DNA testing revealed an entirely unknown species.

Adult male Perrin's beaked whales grow just two large, triangular teeth at the very tip of their lower jaw that protrude outside the closed mouth like miniature tusks and are used for jousting with rivals.
To survive crushing pressures nearly a mile beneath the ocean surface, Perrin's beaked whale can collapse its lungs completely and shunt oxygen-rich blood strictly to its heart and brain.
The throat of Perrin's beaked whale features two deep V-shaped grooves that expand like accordion pleats, allowing the whale to suck squid and deep-sea fish into its mouth like a vacuum cleaner.
To date, not a single confirmed live sighting of Perrin's beaked whale has ever been photographed at sea, making it one of the most mysterious large mammals on Earth.
Eld's deer: Unlike almost any other deer, Eld's deer stags grow lyre-shaped antlers that sweep forward over the brow and backward in one continuous, seamless curve up to four feet long, earning the species the nickname 'brow-antlered deer.'

During the rut, Eld's deer stags wallow in muddy pits and thrash bushes until hanging vines and swamp weeds get tangled in their antlers, wearing the vegetation like a festive crown to intimidate rivals.
The Manipur subspecies of Eld's deer lives strictly on 'phumdis'; thick, floating mats of tangled decaying vegetation and soil on India's Loktak Lake that bob up and down under the deer's hooves.
To keep from sinking through spongy floating islands, the Manipur Eld's deer has evolved splayed, elongated hooves with tough, rubbery undersides that act like snowshoes.
Eld's deer stags shed and regrow their massive sweeps of bone every single year, reaching peak antler size right at the height of the scorching dry season rather than autumn.
Striped dolphin: Famous among sailors for an acrobatic move called 'roto-tailing,' the striped dolphin launches up to twenty feet out of the water while spinning its tail furiously in midair before splashing down.
A bold, paintbrush-like stripe of dark navy blue sweeps from a striped dolphin's eye all the way back to its flipper and anus, looking like custom racing decals on a speedboat.
When disturbed by approaching ships in the eastern tropical Pacific, striped dolphin pods take off at speeds topping thirty miles per hour, earning them the fishermen's nickname 'streakers.'
Inside a striped dolphin's jaws sit up to 100 needle-sharp, conical teeth that interlock to snag slippery lanternfish and luminescent deep-water squid during night dives.
Even in pitch-black depths of 2,000 feet, a striped dolphin coordinates tight group formations using rapid-fire clicks and high-pitched whistles that carry for miles underwater.
African civet: Sporting a black bandit mask across its eyes closely resembling a raccoon's, the nocturnal African civet is actually a distant relative of mongooses and hyenas.
An African civet can safely devour foods that would kill almost any other predator, including rotting carrion, poisonous millipedes, and even venomous puff adders.

Rather than scent-marking at random, an African civet carefully deposits secretions from its perineal glands onto specific 'civetries'; communal latrines and roadside posts at the exact height of a rival's nose.
For centuries in Ethiopia, zibeth, the buttery yellow musk scraped from an African civet's scent pouch, was traded for more than its weight in gold to French and Arabian perfumers.
When threatened, an African civet erects a four-inch-high dorsal crest of coarse black hair from its shoulders to its rump, instantly making itself look twice as large in the moonlight.
Red-shanked douc: Often called the 'costumed ape' because the red-shanked douc looks like it got dressed in the dark, it wears maroon knee-high stockings, white forearm gloves, a black vest, and a powdery golden face framed by a fluffy white beard.
A red-shanked douc's stomach is divided into chambers loaded with specialized bacteria that ferment tough leaves, causing the monkey to burp loudly throughout the day like a miniature cow.
Giving a red-shanked douc sweet, ripe fruit can actually be fatal: the rapid fermentation of sugars in its foregut causes severe bloating and acidosis.
When playing or flirting in the canopy, red-shanked douc troop members pull a 'play face' with eyes squeezed completely shut and mouth wide open while swatting gently at one another.
Instead of descending to streams where pythons and leopards lurk, a red-shanked douc gets almost all of its water by licking morning dew off broad jungle leaves and chewing moisture-rich leaf buds.
Water deer: Completely lacking antlers in both sexes, the male water deer grows a pair of curved, razor-sharp upper canine tusks over two inches long, earning it the spooky nickname 'vampire deer.'

A water deer's impressive fangs aren't fixed rigidly in the jaw; hinged sockets controlled by facial muscles let the buck pull his tusks backward out of the way while chewing grass, then snap them forward for combat.
When startled in tall river reeds, the water deer doesn't bound gracefully like a typical deer, instead rocketing away with rabbit-like hops that flash its white rump.
Whereas nearly all deer give birth to only one or two fawns, female water deer regularly deliver litters of up to five or six tiny spotted offspring at once.
An exceptional swimmer with hollow, buoyant hairs in its coat, the water deer can paddle for several miles across chilly river currents and open estuaries to reach isolated islands.
Dusky hopping mouse: Built like a miniature kangaroo no bigger than an apple, the dusky hopping mouse bounds across sand dunes on oversized hind legs while using its long, tufted tail as a counterbalance.

A dusky hopping mouse never needs to drink a single drop of liquid water in its entire life; its hyper-efficient kidneys produce the most concentrated urine of almost any mammal, recycling moisture synthesized from dry seeds.
Every dusk, the dusky hopping mouse bursts out of a burrow dug five feet deep into cool desert sand, plugging the entrance tunnel from the inside during the day to trap humidity.
Equipped with huge, radar-dish ears and dark, protruding eyes, a dusky hopping mouse can hear the faint rustle of a beetle's legs on windblown sand yards away.
On the center of a dusky hopping mouse's chest sits a specialized sebaceous gland that secretes a musky oil rubbed onto burrow walls to tell family members apart from intruders.
Tenkile: Also known as Scott's tree-kangaroo, the cloud-forest tenkile can drop fifty feet out of a canopy tree onto the rocky ground below and walk away without a scratch.
Unlike ground-dwelling kangaroos that can only move both hind legs together in a hop, the tenkile can move its back feet independently to walk along narrow mossy branches.
At the base of a tenkile's tail sits a permanent, hairless callous pad that acts like a built-in climbing brake, bracing the animal against slippery bark as it ascends.
By the late 1990s, fewer than 100 tenkiles survived in Papua New Guinea's Torricelli Mountains until a historic pact among fifty local villages banned hunting them and tripled their numbers.
A tenkile's thick, chocolate-brown coat grows in a whorl pattern on its shoulders that channels torrential mountain rainwater straight off its back while it sleeps sitting up in the branches.
American red squirrel: Fiercely territorial and famously loud, a single American red squirrel harvests up to 20,000 spruce cones every autumn and piles them into a massive central vault called a 'midden' that can span thirty feet across.
Generations of American red squirrels often inherit the same family midden for decades, as the moist, rotting cone scales keep unpeeled seeds inside fresh for years.

In early spring, the American red squirrel acts as a tiny maple-syrup tapper: it bites V-shaped notches into the bark of sugar maples, leaves for the day to let the sap evaporate into thick sugar, and returns to lick up the syrup.
An American red squirrel harvests deadly poisonous Amanita mushrooms that would kill a human, wedges them into tree forks to dry in the sun for days, and then eats them without harm.
Altruism exists even among feisty American red squirrels: females have been documented adopting and nursing orphaned pups only when the orphans are close genetic relatives.
Abert's squirrel: In winter, the plumes of fur on the tips of an Abert's squirrel's ears grow over an inch and a half long, giving it the unmistakable silhouette of a woodland elf or a miniature lynx.

Almost an Abert's squirrel's entire life is tied to a single tree species, the ponderosa pine, where it builds spherical nests out of twigs, strips the sweet inner bark in winter, and feasts on pine seeds.

The Abert's squirrel populations living on the North and South Rims of the Grand Canyon were separated by the canyon's formation; the isolated North Rim squirrels evolved black bellies and snowy-white tails, becoming the famous 'Kaibab squirrel.'
During heavy Rocky Mountain blizzards, instead of hibernating, several normally solitary Abert's squirrels will pile into the same pine-needle nest to share body heat.
By digging up and eating underground truffle fungi that grow on ponderosa roots, an Abert's squirrel spreads millions of fungal spores in its droppings that help young pine trees absorb water.
Chinkara: The chinkara, a graceful Indian gazelle, gets its name from its high-pitched alarm sneeze, an explosive 'chink!' blasted through its nostrils whenever it spots a leopard or wolf.
Adapted to the blistering Thar Desert, the chinkara can go for weeks without drinking water by grazing on dew-soaked desert melons and succulent leaves before sunrise.
Unlike most antelopes where only males carry weapons, both male and female chinkaras grow ringed, S-shaped horns, though the male's are thicker and longer.
For over five hundred years, the Bishnoi community of Rajasthan has revered the chinkara as sacred, sometimes even nursing orphaned fawns by hand in their homes.
When chased across open scrubland, the chinkara executes 'stotting,' bouncing high into the air with all four legs held stiffly straight to prove to predators that it is too athletic to catch.
Bohor reedbuck: Instead of barking or grunting when danger approaches, the bohor reedbuck blasts a shrill, piercing whistle through its nostrils while bounding away like a rocking horse.
A bohor reedbuck's glossy, straw-yellow coat is coated in natural oils secreted by skin glands, keeping the fur completely water-repellent as it wades through waist-deep African marshes.
Beneath each ear of a bohor reedbuck sits a circular patch of bare, black skin that scientists believe helps release excess heat or diffuse pheromones during territorial displays.
When a predator creeps close, a hiding bohor reedbuck flattens its neck and head flush against the mud and refuses to budge until the hunter almost steps on it.
Only male bohor reedbucks grow short, stout horns that hook sharply forward at the tips like grappling hooks, used for shoving matches in the reeds.
Mountain nyala: Because the mountain nyala lives above 10,000 feet in the misty Bale Mountains of Ethiopia, this spiral-horned antelope remained completely unknown to Western science until 1908.
Despite the mountain nyala's name, DNA reveals it is actually much closer to the greater kudu and bushbuck than to the lowland nyala of southern Africa.

Rather than locking horns in violent collisions that could break a rival's neck, competing mountain nyala bulls circle each other in slow motion with their chins tucked and dorsal crests raised until one backs down.
Old mountain nyala bulls grow majestic lyre-shaped horns with up to two full twists that turn a polished ivory-yellow at the tips from years of rubbing against giant heather trees.
As freezing temperatures grip the alpine moorlands at night, mountain nyala herds descend into giant Erica forests that act as a thermal blanket against subzero winds.
Common genet: Although the common genet purrs, grooms its whiskers, and stalks mice with fully retractable claws like a tabby cat, it is actually a primitive relative of civets and mongooses.
Before the rise of domestic cats in Europe, Medieval nobles and Moorish households kept tamed common genets indoors as prized rat-catchers that slept on silk cushions.
The common genet is the only carnivore capable of squeezing through any gap its narrow skull can pass, thanks to a spine so flexible it can turn 180 degrees inside a hollow tree trunk.
When startled, a common genet can leap six feet straight up from a standstill, using its banded tail, which is just as long as its entire head and body, as a midair rudder.
To mark a nightly hunting trail, a common genet performs a handstand on its front paws so it can press its scent glands higher up on vertical tree trunks.
Tapeti: Also called the Brazilian cottontail, the tapeti is one of the only rabbits native to the tropical rainforests of South America, trading open meadows for tangled riverside undergrowth.
Unlike North American cottontails, the tapeti lacks a fluffy white 'cottontail' puff; its tiny tail is dark brown on both sides and practically invisible.

Instead of digging deep underground warrens that would flood in torrential tropical rains, a mother tapeti weaves a shallow, dome-shaped nursery of dry grass and lines it with fur plucked from her own belly.
A tapeti's ears are noticeably shorter and more rounded than those of desert or grassland rabbits, an adaptation that prevents snags while darting through thorny jungle vines.
Strictly nocturnal, a tapeti freezes like a statue at the slightest rustle in the leaf litter, relying on its mottled orange-and-black coat to vanish against rotting logs.
Hispid hare: Frequently called the 'bristly rabbit,' the hispid hare, an elusive Himalayan foothills dweller, wears an outer coat of stiff, wire-like hairs that feel more like a scrub brush than bunny fur.

For nearly twenty years in the mid-20th century, conservationists feared the hispid hare had gone completely extinct until a live individual was captured in Assam's Barnadi Wildlife Sanctuary in 1971.
The hispid hare's stubby ears are shorter than its own hind feet and curve forward like tiny spoons, hugging the skull as it tunnels through razor-sharp elephant grass over ten feet tall.
Unlike true hares whose babies are born fully furred and ready to run on open ground, the hispid hare digs shallow burrows or takes over abandoned badger holes to shelter its young.
Because the hispid hare lives solely in tall thatch-grass prairies along riverbanks, its survival depends on seasonal monsoons and controlled grass fires that prevent trees from taking over.
Nabarlek: The nabarlek, a pint-sized Australian rock-wallaby, shares an astonishing dental superpower with elephants and manatees: it grows a continuous conveyor belt of up to forty molars that march forward in its jaw as old worn teeth drop out the front.

Why does the three-pound nabarlek need self-replacing teeth? Its favorite food is 'resurrection fern,' a tough desert plant packed with abrasive silica crystals that grind normal teeth down to the gums.
A nabarlek's hind feet have textured, rubbery soles fringed with stiff hairs that grip sun-baked sandstone boulders like high-performance rock-climbing shoes.
During the scorching Kimberley dry season, the nabarlek shelters deep inside cool sandstone caves and rock fissures where temperatures stay twenty degrees cooler than outside.
When bounding across vertical cliff faces at night, a nabarlek swings its brush-tipped tail in wide circles to change direction in midair without losing momentum.
Yangtze finless porpoise: Famous for the permanent, mischievous 'smile' curved across a Yangtze finless porpoise's blunt snout, it is the world's only freshwater porpoise and has become China's beloved river mascot.
In place of a dorsal fin, the Yangtze finless porpoise has a narrow ridge down its back studded with rows of sensitive, wart-like tubercles packed with nerve endings that may sense water currents.
When playful or irritated with tour boats, the Yangtze finless porpoise has been observed rising to the surface and spitting targeted jets of water straight at riverside spectators.

Because a Yangtze finless porpoise's rounded forehead contains a fatty organ called a 'melon' that can change shape, the porpoise can focus beams of sonar clicks like an adjustable flashlight through murky river silt.
Yangtze finless porpoise mothers carry their newborn calves piggyback-style on the rough, textured ridge along their spine, helping the baby breathe during its first weeks in fast river currents.
Sambar deer: Before entering a fight during the rut, a sambar deer stag rears up on his hind legs and sprays his own face and chest with urine, soaking his coarse neck mane in pungent musk.
On the center of a male sambar deer's throat sits a strange, hairless 'sore spot' up to three inches wide that oozes a watery secretion during the breeding season and heals completely afterward.
When a sambar deer stag spots a stalking tiger in the Indian jungle, he stomps his front hoof violently and lets out a metallic, bell-like 'dhank!' bark that alerts every animal within half a mile.
Unlike dainty woodland deer, sambar deer love water so much they regularly swim across ocean channels between coastal islands and submerge up to their nostrils to graze on water lilies.
Instead of branching into many delicate tines, a sambar deer's massive, rugged antlers have only three thick spikes per side that can parry the swipe of a leopard.
Pichi: Known as the dwarf armadillo of Patagonia, the pichi is the only armadillo on Earth capable of entering true hibernation during freezing South American winters.
Along the outer edges of a pichi's leathery carapace runs a row of saw-toothed scales that give its shell the look of an armored medieval shield.
Wait out a rainstorm? The pichi never drinks standing water, obtaining all its hydration from juicy beetle grubs, ants, and desert tubers dug up in sandy steppe soils.
Because a pichi's armor shell cannot roll into a tight ball, a cornered pichi pulls its legs underneath its body and slams its jagged shell flat against the dirt so no fox can flip it over.
If a predator tries to pull a pichi out of its burrow, the pichi wedges its serrated shell edges directly into the tunnel walls like an expanding anchor.
Milne-Edwards' sportive lemur: Milne-Edwards' sportive lemur earned the 'sportive' nickname because when cornered inside its hollow tree, it raises both fists up by its chin and weaves like a prize-fighting boxer ready to throw a punch.

Surviving on a nutrient-poor diet of tough mature leaves, Milne-Edwards' sportive lemur practices 'coprophagy,' re-eating its own soft night droppings to extract vitamins and proteins broken down by gut bacteria the first time through.
Because leaves provide barely any spare calories, Milne-Edwards' sportive lemur has one of the lowest metabolic rates of any primate, spending hours motionless on vertical tree trunks to save energy.
At night, the huge, bulging eyes of Milne-Edwards' sportive lemur reflect headlamp beams like glowing orange marbles as it launches up to fifteen feet backward from one trunk to the next.
Monogamous pairs of Milne-Edwards' sportive lemurs defend their tiny patch of Madagascar rainforest by singing loud, synchronized duets that echo through the trees at dusk.
Beech marten: Across Central Europe, the sleek beech marten is notorious as the 'car-eating marten' because it sneaks under the hoods of parked automobiles at night and chews through warm rubber brake lines and ignition cables.

Why do beech martens chew car wires? When a rival marten scent-marks a warm engine block, the next beech marten to arrive flies into a territorial rage and attacks the hoses that carry the rival's smell.

Also called the 'stone marten,' the beech marten happily swaps deep forests for church steeples, stone barns, and suburban attics, where its midnight roughhousing sounds like footsteps on the ceiling.
You can tell a beech marten apart from the pine marten at a glance by the bright white bib on its throat, which splits into two forks that run down its front legs.
In autumn, the beech marten switches from hunting mice and birds to gorging on sweet cherries, plums, and rosehips, leaving purple-stained droppings on high garden walls to mark its turf.
Black-and-white ruffed lemur: Instead of a black-and-white ruffed lemur mother carrying babies clinging to her belly like other lemurs, she builds a leafy nest sixty feet up in a tree fork and parks her litter of up to six infants there while she forages.

The black-and-white ruffed lemur is the world's largest pollinator: as it plunges its long snout deep into the blossoms of the giant Traveler's Palm to lap up nectar, its fluffy white cheek ruffs get dusted in golden pollen.

Only black-and-white ruffed lemur mothers produce milk rich enough to nourish large lemur litters, and when moving her babies between nests, she picks them up one by one by the scruff of the neck like a housecat.
Entire valleys in Madagascar echo with the black-and-white ruffed lemur's 'roar-shriek chorus,' a deafening group alarm call that rises and falls like a cross between a chainsaw and a siren.

To comb parasites out of a black-and-white ruffed lemur's cloud-soft fur, its lower front teeth are fused into a tiny, forward-tilted 'toothcomb' paired with a secondary cartilage 'sub-tongue' used specifically to clean between the teeth.
Eastern quoll: Even within the exact same litter, eastern quoll pups come in two completely different base colors, either warm fawn-brown or jet-black, both covered in snowy white polka dots.
Though no bigger than a small housecat, the eastern quoll possesses one of the strongest bite forces relative to body size of any living mammal, easily crunching through bone and chitin.

A female eastern quoll gives birth to up to thirty tiny, jellybean-sized embryos at once, yet she has only six teats inside her pouch; only the first six babies to crawl inside and latch on will survive.

After vanishing from the Australian mainland in the 1960s, the eastern quoll survived solely on the island of Tasmania until conservationists began reintroducing fenced populations near Canberra in 2018.
When two eastern quolls square off over a carcass in the dark, they open their jaws to an astonishing 80-degree gape and screech like miniature Tasmanian devils.
Tibetan antelope: Living on the Changtang Plateau at altitudes above 16,000 feet where oxygen is half that at sea level, the Tibetan antelope can still sprint at fifty miles per hour across frozen gravel plains.

Beneath a Tibetan antelope's coarse guard hairs grows 'shahtoosh', meaning 'king of wools' in Persian, the finest mammal underfur on Earth, with individual fibers five times thinner than a human hair.
Inside a Tibetan antelope's bulbous snout sit two inflatable sacs within the nostrils that act like bellows, drawing in huge gulps of thin mountain air with every stride.
Every summer, tens of thousands of pregnant female Tibetan antelopes embark on a 400-mile pilgrimage across snow-swept mountain passes to ancient calving grounds they have used for millennia.

In medieval Tibet, travelers crossing the plateau reported seeing 'unicorns' after spotting male Tibetan antelopes in profile, where their two long, straight horns align so perfectly they look like a single spire.
Southwestern pygmy possum: Weighing less than a standard AA battery, the southwestern pygmy possum survives strictly on a liquid diet of flower nectar and protein-rich pollen harvested from banksia blossoms.
The southwestern pygmy possum's long tongue is tipped with a dense brush of microscopic bristles that soak up nectar like a paintbrush through capillary action.

When cold winter rain or food shortages hit Western Australia, the southwestern pygmy possum curls into a tight ball, drops its body temperature to match the air, and slows its breathing to enter multi-day torpor.
Like a miniature monkey, the southwestern pygmy possum has a fully prehensile tail and opposable, clawless big toes on its hind feet that let it hang upside down from slender twigs.

The southwestern pygmy possum doesn't store extra calories from spring flower blooms around its waist; instead, it packs fat directly into the base of its tail, which swells up like a tiny carrot before lean months.
Blue duiker: Standing barely twelve inches tall at the shoulder, no taller than a bowling pin, the blue duiker is a miniature forest antelope that gets its name from the slate-blue sheen of its sleek coat under filtered jungle light.

Blue duikers form lifelong monogamous pairs that stay together year-round, constantly pressing the crescent-shaped scent glands beneath their eyes against each other's cheeks to share a unified family perfume.
Rather than grazing in the open, a blue duiker shadows troops of monkeys and hornbills moving high in the canopy, waiting below to snap up half-eaten figs and seeds dropped from sixty feet up.
Despite being a hoofed ruminant, the blue duiker occasionally supplements its vegetarian diet by crunching up protein-packed ants, beetles, and even freshly laid bird eggs.
True to the Afrikaans name 'duiker' (meaning 'diver'), at the snap of a twig a blue duiker launches headfirst into impenetrable thorn thickets where eagles and leopards cannot follow.
Dibbler: For 83 years, science believed the freckled dibbler had gone completely extinct, until wildlife photographer Michael Morcombe accidentally caught two in flower-baited traps on Cheynes Beach in 1967.
Instead of running across the ground where foxes lurk, the dibbler scrambles through the intertwined branches of coastal banksia shrubs using a tapering, carrot-shaped tail for balance.
Every single adult male dibbler in certain island populations dies shortly after a frantic two-week mating season, triggered by a surge of stress hormones that shuts down their immune systems.
Ringed around each of a dibbler's eyes is a vivid halo of white fur that makes the tiny nocturnal hunter look perpetually wide-eyed as it pokes its long snout into blossoms for insects and nectar.
Female dibblers lack a true enclosed pouch; instead, up to eight newborn joeys cling directly to exposed teats on her belly, shielded only by folds of skin and dense fur.
Neotropical otter: The nose pad (rhinarium) of the sleek Neotropical otter varies in shape across different river basins, allowing biologists to identify regional populations just by examining nose prints.
Unlike sea otters that float on their backs to crack shellfish, the Neotropical otter hauls crabs and armored catfish onto favorite riverside rocks or logs to crunch them open.
To stay dry in cool mountain torrents from Mexico to Argentina, a Neotropical otter's coat packs an incredible 50,000 interlocking hairs into every square inch of skin.
Instead of digging from scratch, the Neotropical otter prefers moving into natural limestone caves, hollow tree roots overhanging the water, or even abandoned caiman burrows.
While hunting in murky jungle rivers where eyesight fails, a Neotropical otter relies on stiff, forward-swept whiskers that detect the tiny hydrodynamic vortices left behind by a fleeing fish's tail.
Zanzibar red colobus: The Zanzibar red colobus is an island monkey famous for routinely eating charcoal: it steals burnt wood from human kilns and campfires to absorb the toxic phenolic acids found in the young mango and almond leaves it devours.
Unlike almost all other primates outside of the great apes, young Zanzibar red colobus monkeys keep nursing from their mothers until they are up to four years old.
A Zanzibar red colobus lacks working thumbs entirely; each hand has only four long, curved fingers that snap over branches like a gymnast's grip hook as it leaps through the canopy.
A Zanzibar red colobus's expressive black face is framed by a flamboyant halo of shocking white hair that looks like Einstein's hairdo and a bright pink stripe across its lips.
Waiters and tourists at resorts on Unguja Island often watch Zanzibar red colobus troops stroll right across hotel verandahs to raid ornamental garden trees and charcoal grills.
Mountain pygmy possum: The mountain pygmy possum, a two-ounce marvel, is the only Australian marsupial that lives exclusively above the winter snowline and enters true, seven-month hibernation beneath the snowpack.

Every spring in the Victorian Alps, the mountain pygmy possum's primary feast flies right into its living room: billions of migrating Bogong moths shelter inside the same boulder fields, offering a butter-rich protein buffet.

Right before winter arrives, the mountain pygmy possum eats enough moths and mountain plum-pine seeds to double its body weight, dropping its heart rate from 300 beats per minute to just a few beats while hibernating.
Before eating a Bogong moth, the mountain pygmy possum deftly holds the insect in its tiny forepaws like a corn cob, biting off the powdery wings and legs to swallow only the fat-filled abdomen.
Until 1966, the mountain pygmy possum was known strictly from Pleistocene fossils and considered extinct for thousands of years, until a live one wandered into a ski lodge at Mount Hotham.
Vancouver Island marmot: Found nowhere else on Earth except the alpine meadows of a single Canadian island, the chocolate-brown Vancouver Island marmot announces predators with a piercing, bird-like whistle heard half a mile away.

When emerging from eight months of hibernation under twenty feet of snow, Vancouver Island marmot family members greet each other by pressing their noses together and locking teeth in a gentle 'play-bite' handshake.
By 2003, fewer than thirty wild Vancouver Island marmots remained on the planet before a heroic captive-breeding and mountain-release effort pulled them back from the brink.
Over the course of a summer, a Vancouver Island marmot's rich espresso-colored coat sun-bleaches into a patchwork of cinnamon and gold until it molts into fresh dark fur in July.
To wait out the cold, the Vancouver Island marmot spends roughly 210 days a year asleep inside deep rock-crevice burrows plugged from the inside with a mortar of mud, grass, and pebbles.
Hooded seal: To impress females or intimidate rivals on the pack ice, a hooded seal bull inflates his elastic nasal septum through one nostril until a bright crimson balloon twice the size of a football bulges out of his nose.
When a bull hooded seal shakes his head with his red nasal bladder inflated, he produces an underwater 'pinging' roar that echoes for miles beneath the Arctic ice floes.
Female hooded seals produce the richest milk of any mammal on Earth, over 60 percent pure fat, thicker than heavy whipping cream or mayonnaise.
Because hooded seal milk is so calorie-dense, a newborn 'blueback' pup doubles its weight from fifty to one hundred pounds in just four days; the shortest nursing period of any mammal.

Directly after a mother hooded seal weans her pup on day four, she mates in the water and disappears to dive over half a mile deep for Greenland halibut, leaving the plump pup to learn to swim completely on its own.
Alaska marmot: Living on windswept talus slopes in the Brooks Range above the Arctic Circle, whole Alaska marmot families hibernate together in a single communal chamber for up to nine months of the year.
Before Alaska marmots seal themselves in for the winter in September, family members pack the burrow entrance with a concrete-like plug made of chewed tundra grass, soil, and their own dung.
During nine months underground, Alaska marmots periodically wake up every three weeks just long enough to shiver their body temperatures up and use a separate underground latrine chamber.
In Alaska Native Inupiat tradition, where the Alaska marmot is known as 'Siksrikpak,' its thick, frost-resistant pelt was prized for sewing warm winter parkas.
When Alaska marmot mothers emerge onto snow-covered rocks in May, they have already given birth underground and nurse their pups for weeks before a single green blade of grass appears outside.
Grivet: Male grivets are famous among primatologists for their 'red, white, and blue' rear display: a bright turquoise scrotum framed by snowy white thigh fur and a crimson streak around the base of the tail.

Grivets use distinct, vocabulary-like alarm calls for different predators: a 'leopard bark' sends the whole troop sprinting up to the thinnest treetop branches, while an 'eagle cough' makes everyone dive down into dense bushes.
Along the Blue Nile in Ethiopia, grivet troops have lived alongside human settlements for thousands of years and appear in ancient Egyptian frescoes wearing jeweled collars as household pets.
Each cheek of a grivet is framed by sweeping tufts of pure white whiskers that curve upward past the ears like muttonchops against a soot-black face.
Although primarily fruit-and-seed eaters, savanna grivet troops waiting by waterholes will wade into the shallows to catch freshwater crabs and frogs with their bare hands.
Steenbok: The steenbok, a dainty southern African antelope, is the only ruminant that scrapes a neat hole in the soil before urinating or defecating and then carefully buries its droppings like a fastidious housecat.

Why does the steenbok bury its waste? By covering the pile with dirt using its front hooves, it hides its scent trail from tracking jackals while simultaneously infusing its interdigital pedal glands with its own territorial marker.
When spotted by a cheetah or martial eagle, instead of trying to outrun the hunter across open plains, a steenbok frequently dives headfirst down an aardvark burrow and waits underground.
A steenbok's huge, paddle-shaped ears are nearly as long as its entire head and are laced with dark veins and white inner stripes that radiate desert heat and pick up the footsteps of predators.
Capable of surviving in the Kalahari without ever visiting a waterhole, the steenbok digs up moisture-packed underground tubers and bulbs with its needle-sharp front hooves.
Tehuantepec jackrabbit: Restricted to a tiny strip of coastal grassy dunes and palms in Oaxaca, Mexico, the rare Tehuantepec jackrabbit is easily recognized by two bold black stripes that run from the base of its giant ears down onto its nape.
Unlike almost all other hares, a Tehuantepec jackrabbit's flanks and rump are bright snow-white rather than brown, flashing in the moonlight as it zigzags across coastal lagoons.

To beat the blistering tropical sun, a Tehuantepec jackrabbit's translucent six-inch ears are packed with blood vessels that dilate when warm, acting like car radiators whenever a sea breeze blows past.
Rather than digging burrows in the loose sand, the Tehuantepec jackrabbit kicks out a shallow 'form' beneath prickly nopal cacti or thorny shrubs where coyotes hesitate to stick their noses.
When startled at dusk, a Tehuantepec jackrabbit can bound ten feet in a single stride while hitting speeds of thirty-five miles per hour across uneven sandbanks.
Kit fox: Though weighing less than a Chihuahua, often under five pounds, the desert-dwelling kit fox sports enormous, bat-like ears that take up a huge fraction of its head to hear kangaroo rats tunneling underground.
The soles of a kit fox's paws are completely covered in dense, stiff fur that acts as both insulated boots against 150-degree desert sand and snowshoes for traction on loose dunes.
How does a carnivorous kit fox survive in Death Valley without a drop of fresh water? It extracts 100 percent of its moisture from the body fluids of the rodents and insects it eats.

One mated pair of kit foxes may rotate among more than a dozen different underground dens within a single year, each dug with multiple keyhole-shaped entrances just narrow enough to block badgers and coyotes.
Unlike red foxes that hunt alone, kit fox fathers stay closely bonded to their mates and haul food back to the den every night while the mother nurses the pups.
Small-toothed sportive lemur: True to the small-toothed sportive lemur's name, its upper incisor teeth shrink and fall out completely by adulthood, leaving a toothless gap on top while its lower teeth form a grooming comb.

When sleeping during the day inside tangled vines, a small-toothed sportive lemur rolls up into a tight furry ball with its face tucked between its knees so predators mistake it for a wasp nest or a burl on a trunk.
Because a small-toothed sportive lemur's diet of tough rainforest leaves is so low in calories, it spends less than a third of the night moving and the rest sitting completely still like a gargoyle.
By springing off coiled, frog-like hind legs, a small-toothed sportive lemur can leap vertically between tree trunks without ever touching the forest floor.
A small-toothed sportive lemur's large, forward-facing ears can swivel independently like twin satellite dishes to pinpoint the wingbeats of nocturnal owls in the dark canopy.
Golden bandicoot: To escape the blistering 110-degree heat of northwestern Australia's Kimberley plateau, the toaster-sized golden bandicoot spends the day hidden inside deep sandstone rock crevices.
At night, a golden bandicoot uses its long, conical snout and dagger-like front claws to jackhammer up to fifty conical pits in the soil, sniffing out truffles, termites, and Witchetty grubs.

The golden bandicoot holds one of the fastest gestation records in the mammal kingdom: a mother carries her babies for just twelve days before giving birth to tiny pink joeys that crawl into her backward-facing pouch.
Why does a golden bandicoot's pouch open toward its tail instead of its head? So the mother doesn't shovel dirt and sand straight onto her nursing babies while furiously digging!
When a golden bandicoot joey finally leaves the pouch at eight weeks old, it is already nearly half its mother's size and ready to breed just weeks later.
Eastern grey kangaroo: At speeds over thirty-five miles per hour, a hopping eastern grey kangaroo actually uses less energy the faster it goes: its giant Achilles tendons stretch and snap back like rubber pogo sticks with every bound.

Each time an eastern grey kangaroo's feet leave the ground, its internal organs slam downward and pull air into its lungs; when it lands, the organs slide forward and push the air out, turning its whole body into a living bellows.

An eastern grey kangaroo mother can undergo 'embryonic diapause,' simultaneously raising a hopping toddler outside the pouch, nursing a hairless pink newborn inside, and keeping a third microscopic embryo paused on standby.

Even more remarkably, an eastern grey kangaroo mother's body produces two completely different formulas of milk at the exact same time from adjacent teats: high-fat milk for the older joey and high-carbohydrate milk for the newborn.
Unlike human legs, an eastern grey kangaroo's hind legs cannot move independently on land, yet if it jumps into a river to swim, it kicks each leg alternately like a dog paddle.
Caspian seal: Landlocked hundreds of miles from the nearest ocean, the Caspian seal is the only marine mammal found in the Caspian Sea, the world's largest inland body of water.

How did the Caspian seal, a true Arctic seal, end up trapped in a desert-rimmed sea? Ancestors of the ringed seal swam south during the last Ice Age when glacial meltwater formed giant inland rivers across Eurasia.
Every winter, Caspian seal mothers haul out onto freezing, wind-swept ice sheets in the shallow northern Caspian to give birth to pups wrapped in fluffy, snow-white 'lanugo' coats.
During the scorching summer months when the northern shallows warm up, Caspian seals migrate south and dive over 650 feet deep into cold abyssal basins to hunt kilka sprat.
When resting at sea without ice or beaches nearby, Caspian seals bob vertically at the surface like corks, a behavior called 'bottling', sleeping with just the tips of their noses above water.
Gee's golden langur: For decades, the silky, cream-gold Gee's golden langur was dismissed as a mythical 'golden monkey' of Himalayan folklore until naturalist E. P. Gee photographed a troop along the Assam-Bhutan border in 1953.
A Gee's golden langur's coat actually changes color with the seasons, shifting from pale ivory in the scorching monsoon summer to a deep, glowing apricot-gold when winter chills the hills.

Living thirty to a hundred feet up in the treetops, Gee's golden langur is so deeply adapted to canopy life that troops crossed the Brahmaputra tributaries using man-made suspension bridges rather than swimming.

In 2019, the last lone male Gee's golden langur isolated on Umananda, the world's smallest inhabited river island in Assam, made global headlines for befriending Hindu temple priests who fed him daily.
Newborn Gee's golden langurs are born pure snow-white or dark smoky-brown, allowing every female in the troop to spot the infant immediately and take turns babysitting.
Allen's swamp monkey: Unlike almost all monkeys that panic in deep water, Allen's swamp monkey dives completely underwater and swims like an otter whenever an eagle or python attacks.
Between the fingers and toes of Allen's swamp monkey stretches partial webbing that acts like built-in swim fins as it paddles through flooded swamp forests and scoops up shrimp and aquatic beetles.
When a female Allen's swamp monkey is ready to mate, the bare skin on her rump inflates into a rosy-pink cushion, signalling fertility through the dim swamp understory.

Allen's swamp monkey was first described to Western science in 1907 not from a wild expedition, but after zoologist Joel Asaph Allen spotted a live captive monkey sitting in the London Zoo whose species nobody recognized.

At dusk, troops of up to forty Allen's swamp monkeys always gather in waterside branches overhanging deep rivers so that if a leopard climbs their sleeping tree at night, they can drop straight into the water.
Cacomistle: Often called the tropical twin of the ringtail, the cacomistle gets its name straight from the Aztec Nahuatl word 'tlahcomiztli,' meaning 'half-cat' or 'half-mountain-lion.'
A cacomistle's ankles are double-jointed and can rotate a full 180 degrees backward, allowing the cacomistle to sprint headfirst down vertical tree trunks just as fast as it climbs up.
A cacomistle's extravagant black-and-white banded tail is longer than its entire head and body combined, fluffing up into a giant bottle-brush when startled to confuse predators.
The cacomistle has non-retractable, sharp claws built specifically for gripping wet, moss-covered cloud-forest bark at night, unlike its dry-canyon cousin the ringtail.
While curling up to sleep inside a high tree hollow during the day, a cacomistle wraps its plush striped tail completely around its face like a built-in eye mask and scarf.
Lechwe: Built for life in waist-deep African floodplains like the Okavango Delta, a lechwe's hindquarters sit noticeably higher than its shoulders, giving it an awkward slope on dry land but turbo-charged leverage when bounding through water.
Because running through knee-deep marshes is exhausting for lions and wild dogs, a fleeing lechwe splashes straight into the swamp and bounds across the water in long, flat-trajectory leaps.
A lechwe's elongated hooves can splay wide apart like rubber tongs to prevent sinking into soft river mud, while an oily coating on its lower leg fur prevents waterlogging.
During the breeding season, male lechwe gather on small dry islands called 'leks' to spar with their long, lyre-shaped ringed horns while dozens of females watch from the water's edge.
As annual floodwaters rise and fall across the plains, lechwe herds of thousands march back and forth right along the water's edge to feast on freshly exposed, protein-rich marsh grasses.
Pink fairy armadillo: Smaller than a dollar bill and weighing just four ounces, the pink fairy armadillo is the smallest armadillo in the world and looks like a cross between a mole and a piece of strawberry sushi.

Why is a pink fairy armadillo's shell bubblegum pink? A dense network of blood vessels runs right underneath its translucent, paper-thin armor plate, flushing bright rose to dump excess body heat or turning pale to conserve warmth.

Unlike any other armadillo, a pink fairy armadillo's flexible dorsal shell isn't attached along its flanks; it is fused to the spine by just a thin membrane down the center, leaving fluffy white fur exposed underneath like a saddle blanket.

The pink fairy armadillo literally 'swims' through loose desert sand in central Argentina, using its oversized front claws to scoop dirt away while its flat, vertical butt-plate tamps the collapsing tunnel closed behind it.

The vertical, disc-shaped shield on a pink fairy armadillo's rear end, called a 'pelvic buckler', acts as a living cork: once inside a burrow, the armadillo plugs the tunnel with its armored backside so no predator or ant swarm can get in.
Northern quoll: Adult males of the hyper-aggressive northern quoll are 'semelparous'; every single male in the wild dies of sheer exhaustion within two weeks of his very first mating season.
Driven by a massive spike of testosterone, breeding male northern quolls stop eating, lose half their fur, develop open sores, and roam miles every night fighting rivals until their organs give out.

When toxic cane toads invaded northern Australia, northern quolls were wiped out in droves after biting the poisonous amphibians, until scientists opened 'toad-smart schools' using miniature toad-sausages laced with nausea-inducing salt to teach wild quolls to leave toads alone.
On the soles of a northern quoll's feet sit striated, tire-tread pads that allow this housecat-sized hunter to scramble up sheer sandstone cliffs and eucalyptus trunks.
Despite weighing barely two pounds, the northern quoll fearlessly pounces on venomous king brown snakes, monitor lizards, and giant centipedes.
North American deermouse: The big-eyed North American deermouse is a marathon swimmer and climber that stores winter seed caches inside abandoned bird nests, hollow logs, and even the boots of unheated mountain cabins.

North American deermouse populations living at 14,000 feet on the summits of the Rocky Mountains have evolved a mutant hemoglobin gene that binds oxygen tightly in thin air where lowlanders would pass out.
To stay warm during subzero winter nights without hibernating, up to a dozen normally solitary North American deermice will huddle together in a tight, shivering sphere inside a single tree hollow.

When a mother North American deermouse needs to evacuate her nest in a hurry, her blind, nursing pups clamp onto her teats with such an iron grip that she can sprint away dragging the entire litter behind her like a train.
When agitated or warning mates inside a dark burrow, a North American deermouse rapidly drums its front paws against a dry leaf or twig to create a buzzing, insect-like trill.
European hamster: Forget tiny cage pets: the wild European hamster grows as large as a guinea pig, over a foot long, and has a midnight-black belly that serves as aposematic warning coloration.

Why would a hamster need warning colors? When cornered by a fox, dog, or human, a wild European hamster rears up on its hind legs, inflates its cheek pouches with air to look huge, grinds its teeth, and launches five feet into the air straight at its attacker's face.

A European hamster's black-bellied coloring is a classic natural defense shared with honey badgers and zorillas, signaling to predators that this pint-sized brawler will bite to the bone rather than run.

Inside a European hamster's multi-room underground apartment, complete with a separate bedroom, bathroom, and pantry, a single hamster can hoard up to 140 pounds of grain, beans, and potatoes for winter.
How does a European hamster carry 140 pounds of food? Its elastic cheek pouches stretch all the way back to its shoulder blades, letting it haul two ounces of wheat in a single trip.
White-nosed saki: Even among Amazonian primates, the white-nosed saki stands out like a clown in formalwear: jet-black shaggy fur from head to toe paired with a bright bubblegum-pink nose and upper lip.
Rather than eating soft, sweet pulp, the white-nosed saki is a 'seed predator' armed with thick, chisel-like canine teeth that crack open hard, unripe jungle nuts as tough as macadamias.
Known to Brazilian locals as 'flying monkeys,' a white-nosed saki can launch thirty feet horizontally across open gaps between canopy trees with its bushy tail streaming behind like a parachute.
To waterproof its long, coarse coat against daily Amazon downpours, the white-nosed saki grooms itself with oily secretions and hangs over branches like a furry umbrella.
Bonded pairs of white-nosed sakis strengthen their relationship by sharing food mouth-to-mouth and weaving their long, non-prehensile tails together while sleeping side by side.
Small Japanese mole: Tunneling through the volcanic soils of Honshu and Kyushu, the velvet-furred small Japanese mole has no external ears at all and eyes hidden entirely beneath skin.

A small Japanese mole's front paws are permanently rotated outward like twin snow shovels and equipped with an extra, sickle-shaped 'sixth thumb' bone (the os falciforme) that widens the digging palm.
When a small Japanese mole stores live earthworms in its underground pantry for later, it bites the worm's head nerve ganglion to paralyze it without killing it, keeping the meat fresh for weeks.
Because underground tunnels are dangerously low in oxygen and high in carbon dioxide, a small Japanese mole's blood contains extra-high levels of specialized hemoglobin that prevents suffocation.

A small Japanese mole's velvet fur has no 'grain'; the hairs stand straight up on miniature ball-and-socket follicles so the mole can sprint backward through tight clay pipes just as smoothly as forward.
Bush dog: Looking more like an otter crossed with a badger than a typical canine, the stubby-legged Amazonian bush dog has fully webbed feet and dives underwater to chase down giant rodents.

A pack of ten-pound bush dogs can take down a 100-pound capybara or a flightless rhea six times their weight by working as a relay team: half the pack chases the prey on land toward the river while the other half waits in ambush in the water.
To stay in touch while weaving through dense jungle undergrowth where bush dogs cannot see one another, packmates emit continuous high-pitched bird-like peeps and whistles.
Female bush dogs mark territory by backing right up to a tree trunk and kicking their hind legs straight up into a vertical handstand while spraying urine over three feet off the ground.

Western scientists first discovered the bush dog as an extinct Ice Age fossil in Brazilian caves in 1842, only to be stunned years later when indigenous hunters showed them living packs in the forest.
Dall's porpoise: Clocked at speeds up to thirty-four miles per hour, the robust black-and-white Dall's porpoise is the fastest small cetacean on the planet, easily outrunning killer whales.
When a Dall's porpoise races near the surface, its blunt head and dorsal fin slice the water so violently that they throw up a distinct hollow cone of spray known to mariners as a 'rooster tail.'
Because a Dall's porpoise's stark black-and-white color pattern looks just like an orca's, generations of North Pacific fishermen mistakenly believed Dall's porpoises were baby killer whales.
Hyperactive around moving vessels, a Dall's porpoise loves to ride the bow waves of fast ships, only to lose interest and swim away the moment a boat slows down below fifteen knots.
Unlike dolphins that whistle in frequencies humans can hear, Dall's porpoise echolocates using ultra-high-frequency narrow-band clicks well above the range of both human and killer whale hearing.
Shepherd's beaked whale: Shepherd's beaked whale retains a full crocodile-like row of up to fifty functional teeth in both jaws, whereas every other known beaked whale has lost almost all its teeth except for two fighting tusks.

Shepherd's beaked whale is so vanishingly rare in the icy Southern Ocean that for nearly seventy years after its discovery in 1933, knowledge of the species came strictly from decaying carcasses washed onto remote beaches.
At sea, a Shepherd's beaked whale's creamy diagonal body bands and long, bottle-nosed beak give it a striking resemblance to a giant thirty-foot dolphin.
When a Shepherd's beaked whale breaches out of sub-Antarctic swells, it launches half its massive body clear of the waves at a forty-five-degree angle before crashing back onto its side.
Deep-sea squid beaks and bottom-dwelling fish otoliths found in the stomachs of stranded Shepherd's beaked whales show that they hunt nearly a mile down along deep underwater canyon walls.
Collared pika: The collared pika, a fist-sized boulder-dweller of the Alaskan mountains, spends all summer acting as an alpine farmer: it harvests up to fifty trips of wildflowers and grasses a day and spreads them on sun-warmed rocks to cure into dry 'haypiles' so they don't mold in winter.

Sometimes a collared pika incorporates toxic alpine plants into its winter haypile; the natural toxins preserve the stack from rotting while slowly breaking down over months until the leaves become safe to eat in midwinter.
During harsh summers when flowers are scarce, collared pikas have been caught raiding dead birds among the rocks to eat the protein-rich brains.
Around the collared pika's neck sits a distinct collar of smoky gray fur that inspired its name and helps break up its outline against speckled granite talus.
Because it lacks sweat glands and wears a thick winter coat year-round, a collared pika can die of heatstroke if exposed to temperatures as mild as 78 degrees Fahrenheit for just an hour.
Crabeater seal: Despite a crabeater seal's name, this Antarctic seal doesn't eat a single crab! Around 95 percent of its diet consists of tiny pink Antarctic krill, which early 19th-century whalers referred to as 'krabben.'

A crabeater seal's cheek teeth are arguably the most intricate in the entire mammal kingdom: each tooth is carved into five interlocking, multi-pronged lobes that mesh together when the jaw closes like a kitchen strainer.
To feed, the crabeater seal gulps a mouthful of krill-filled seawater and blows the water back out through the gaps in its ornate sieve-teeth, trapping the crustaceans inside.
Up to 80 percent of adult crabeater seals carry long, parallel rake scars across their silver coats; souvenirs of narrow escapes from the jaws of leopard seals and killer whales.
With an estimated population in the millions across the Southern Ocean pack ice, the crabeater seal is the most abundant large wild mammal on Earth after humans.
Greater stick-nest rat: Called 'Wopilkara' by indigenous Australians, the chinchilla-soft greater stick-nest rat is an architectural genius that weaves fortress-like mansions of intertwined sticks up to three feet high and six feet wide.
Generations of greater stick-nest rat family members inherit and expand the same ancestral stick-house for centuries, cementing the branches together with pebbles and sticky, sun-baked urine.

In arid rock overhangs where rain never washes greater stick-nest rat nests away, the hardened urine, known as 'amberat', turns as hard as epoxy resin and preserves plant seeds and pollen for over 10,000 years.
Despite looking like a plump rat, the greater stick-nest rat has oversized, teddy-bear ears, a blunt nose, and a gentle disposition; it almost never bites even when picked up by researchers.

Wiped out across the entire Australian mainland by introduced cats and foxes by the 1930s, the greater stick-nest rat was saved from the last 1,000 survivors clinging to two tiny offshore islands in South Australia.
Emperor tamarin: How did the squirrel-sized Amazonian emperor tamarin end up named after a German monarch? When Swiss zoologist Émil Goeldi received the first museum skins in 1907, he jokingly dubbed it 'imperator' because its sweeping white mustache looked just like Kaiser Wilhelm II's.

In a twist on primate family life, a female emperor tamarin normally gives birth to twins that weigh nearly a quarter of her own body weight, and then hands them straight to the father and older brothers to carry on their backs all day.

Troops of emperor tamarins regularly team up with saddleback tamarins in the same forest: the emperor tamarins stay high in the upper canopy to flush out flying katydids, while the saddlebacks patrol the lower branches to catch whatever drops.

While virtually all male emperor tamarins have colorblind two-color vision like a dog, many females carry an extra X-chromosome gene that gives them full human-like trichromatic color vision for spotting ripe fruit.
An emperor tamarin's hands and feet lack flat primate nails (except on the big toe) and instead sport sharp, curved claws that let the half-pound acrobat cling vertically to wide tree trunks.
Bearded seal: Every spring beneath the Arctic pack ice, male bearded seals sing haunting, otherworldly courtship ballads; long, warbling trills that spiral downward in pitch for over a minute and can be heard twelve miles away underwater.
A bearded seal's dense bush of pale facial whiskers contains more than ten times the nerve endings of land mammals, curling into dramatic spiral ringlets whenever they dry out in the air.
Swimming just inches above the muddy seafloor, a bearded seal uses its super-sensitive whiskers like fingers to feel for buried clams, then blasts a jet of water from its mouth to uncover them.
Once a bearded seal exposes a clam on the seabed, it sucks the soft meat right out of the shell like a vacuum cleaner without swallowing a single shard of broken shell.
Unlike most seals that have two teats, the female bearded seal has four, allowing her newborn pup to pack on three pounds of blubber every single day on the drifting ice.
Monjon: Weighing barely three pounds, less than a bag of sugar, the monjon (or Warabi) is the smallest of all rock-wallabies and lives only among the rugged sandstone gorges of the North Kimberley.

So secret and nocturnal is the monjon's lifestyle among labyrinthine boulder piles that Western scientists had no idea it existed until 1973, though local Kwini Aboriginal people had known it for millennia.
When bounding across vertical sandstone cliffs at night, the monjon raises its bottle-brush tail straight over its head like a scorpion's stinger to startle rivals or predators.
During the bone-dry tropical winter when temperatures soar past 100 degrees, the monjon retreats into deep subterranean rock crevices where humidity stays above 80 percent.
