Like its cousin the nabarlek, the monjon has padded hind feet that lack claws on the fourth toe and instead feature rough, pebbled skin that grips slick quartz rock like sandpaper.
Moonrat: Despite a moonrat's name, the moonrat is not a rodent at all; it is the world's largest member of the hedgehog family, trading sharp spines for coarse black-and-white fur and reaching two feet from nose to tail.

Anyone walking near a moonrat in the Southeast Asian jungle smells it long before seeing it: its anal glands broadcast a pungent odor universally described as rotting garlic, spoiled onions, and stale sweat.
A moonrat's foul ammonia-and-garlic stench acts like an invisible force field, warning civets, snakes, and leopards that this nocturnal prowler tastes every bit as terrible as it smells.
Whereas most hedgehogs stick to dry land, the moonrat loves swamp forests and frequently wades into streams to snap up frogs, freshwater crabs, and fish.
A moonrat's long, flexible, pink snout twitches constantly as it pokes into rotting logs, shielding a mouthful of forty-four needle-sharp teeth.
Roborovski hamster: Measuring just two inches long, roughly the size of a golf ball, the Gobi Desert's Roborovski hamster is the smallest hamster in the world and is born no bigger than a jellybean.
Above each of a Roborovski hamster's dark eyes sits a stark white spot that looks exactly like an expressive pair of cartoon eyebrows, flashing to communicate with mates in dim burrow tunnels.

Even though it fits in the palm of a child's hand, a wild Roborovski hamster runs the human equivalent of four marathons every single night, covering up to ten miles across desert sand in search of seeds.

First collected by Russian explorer Lieutenant Vsevolod Roborovski during an 1894 expedition across the Tibetan frontier, every pet Roborovski hamster in the world today descends from a tiny group brought to London Zoo in the 1960s.
Instead of kicking sand out with bare paws, the Roborovski hamster has densely furred soles that let it glide effortlessly over shifting desert dunes without sinking.
Taruca: Also called the North Andean huemul, the stocky taruca is a mountain deer that lives along rocky cliffs and glacial valleys between 11,000 and 16,000 feet high in the Andes.
Both male and female tarucas wear a bold, pitch-black Y-shaped mask across their faces that absorbs harsh high-altitude UV glare off snowfields, much like an athlete's eye-black grease.
Unlike almost all deer where females are hornless and weaponless, both male and female tarucas grow a pair of sharp upper canine fangs in addition to the buck's forked antlers.
A taruca's short, muscular legs give it a low center of gravity that allows it to bound across loose scree slopes and razor-thin cliff ledges like a mountain goat.
When tarucas graze in groups among highland boulders, a single older female always stands guard on the highest rock pinnacle, whistling a sharp alarm and stamping her foot if a puma approaches.
Sunda flying lemur: The Sunda flying lemur's name is a double lie: it cannot fly (it glides), and it isn't a lemur! Geneticists discovered that colugos are actually the closest living relatives to all primates, including humans.

A Sunda flying lemur's furry gliding membrane, the patagium, is the most complete of any mammal on Earth, stretching from its chin to the tips of all twenty fingers and toes and all the way to the tip of its tail like a living wingsuit.

A mother Sunda flying lemur can glide over 450 feet between rainforest trees, longer than a football field, while losing barely thirty feet of altitude, even with a nursing baby clinging inside her folded belly membrane.

A Sunda flying lemur's lower incisor teeth look like nothing else in nature: each tooth is split into up to twenty tiny, parallel prongs like a miniature hair comb, used both to strain soft plant sap and to comb parasites out of its fur.
Because a Sunda flying lemur's sprawling glide membrane gets in the way on flat ground, it is completely helpless on the forest floor and climbs tree trunks with awkward, lurching two-footed hops.
European otter: The European otter boasts the densest coat in Europe, up to 450,000 hairs per square inch, arranged in two interlocking layers that trap a permanent blanket of dry, warm air right against its skin even in freezing winter rivers.

When hunting along rocky sea coasts in Scotland or Norway, the European otter must still visit freshwater streams every day to wash salt crystals out of its coat so its fur doesn't lose its waterproof insulation.

Instead of scratching the ground to mark territory, the European otter deposits neat piles of sweet-smelling droppings called 'spraints', which smell surprisingly like jasmine tea or freshly cut hay, on prominent boulders.
Equipped with muscular valves that seal its ears and nostrils shut the instant it dives, the European otter can hold its breath for four minutes while chasing eels under river ice.
Each European otter leaves behind five-toed footprints in river mud and builds hidden riverside dens called 'holts' tucked inside the flooded root cages of ancient willow and alder trees.
Pacific white-sided dolphin: Nicknamed 'hookfin porpoises' and 'lag' (short for the scientific genus Lagenorhynchus) by Pacific sailors, the athletic Pacific white-sided dolphin has a two-toned dorsal fin that curves backward like a breaking ocean wave.

The Pacific white-sided dolphin is one of the only wild cetaceans observed turning back to rescue an injured pod-mate, with companions swimming underneath a wounded friend to buoy them up to the surface to breathe.
Super-pods of up to 2,000 Pacific white-sided dolphins gather off the coast of British Columbia and California, turning the ocean surface into a boiling froth with synchronized flips and belly-flops.
Unlike many coastal dolphins, the Pacific white-sided dolphin has dark charcoal rings around its eyes and two creamy white 'suspenders' sweeping from its forehead down along its flanks.
In just sixty seconds, a diving Pacific white-sided dolphin can plunge 600 feet into dark canyon waters to herd schools of anchovies and market squid into tight bait balls.
Pampas deer: During the rut, a male pampas deer produces a scent from his rear hooves so overwhelming, resembling concentrated garlic and burnt rubber, that naturalists including Charles Darwin reported smelling a stag from over a mile away.
Today, fewer than one percent of the pampas deer's original South American grassland habitat remains untouched, yet isolated populations still thrive inside Brazil's vast flooded Pantanal wetlands.

When a pampas deer mother spots a maned wolf or puma stalking her fawn, she performs a 'broken-leg dance,' limping noisily away in full view to lure the predator after her while her spotted baby freezes flat in the grass.
Inquisitive rather than skittish, a pampas deer will often stand up on its hind legs like a kangaroo to peer over tall pampas grass plumes at passing riders.
Every pampas deer fawn is born with rows of creamy white spots that vanish completely by three months of age, replaced by a sleek reddish-tan coat.
Djungarian hamster: Commonly known as the 'winter white dwarf hamster,' a Djungarian hamster's brown-and-black summer fur transforms into a snowy-white camouflage coat as autumn daylight shrinks across the Siberian steppes.

Rather than sleeping through the entire winter in deep hibernation, the Djungarian hamster practices 'daily torpor', dropping its body temperature to sixty degrees for a few hours each morning to save calories before waking up to snack on cached seeds.
Even the soles of a Djungarian hamster's tiny paws and the inside of its ears are covered in dense white fur to prevent frostbite while tunneling under snowdrifts at minus-forty degrees.
Both Djungarian hamster parents share nursery duty in the wild: the father helps clean newborn pups, keeps the nest warm while the mother forages, and even assists during birth.
Along a Djungarian hamster's spine runs a sharp, dark racing stripe that stays visible even when the rest of its body turns winter-white.
Mountain degu: Unlike almost all small rodents, which are creatures of the night, the mountain degu is strictly diurnal and has retinas tuned to see ultraviolet light.

Why does a mountain degu need UV vision? Fresh degu urine reflects ultraviolet rays like neon paint, allowing colonies to read each other's scent trails and territorial borders at a glance across sun-bleached rocks!
If a hawk or fox grabs a mountain degu by the tail, the outer skin and fur slip right off like a glove, a trick called 'degloving', while the degu escapes and chews off the bare vertebrae later.
Unlike a lizard's tail, a mountain degu's tail never regenerates once lost, so a stub-tailed degu has used up its one get-out-of-jail-free card.
A mountain degu's figure-eight-shaped molar teeth give its whole family (Octodontidae) its name, partnered with bright orange front incisors colored by iron-hard enamel.
Bornean ferret-badger: Found only on the misty, 10,000-foot slopes of Mount Kinabalu and neighboring peaks in Borneo, the Bornean ferret-badger looks like a miniature badger stretched out onto a ferret's body.
When cornered by a clouded leopard or dog, the Bornean ferret-badger combines a vicious bite with a skunk-like secret weapon, firing a pungent, foul-smelling liquid from its anal glands.
The Bornean ferret-badger's rubbery, pig-like snout projects well past its lower jaw, acting as a built-in trowel for rooting through mossy mountain leaf litter after earthworms and beetles.
Long, non-retractable white claws on the Bornean ferret-badger's front paws are curved like garden picks to rip open rotting logs and dig sleeping burrows beneath rhododendron roots.

Despite living in cold, wet cloud forests high above the tropical lowlands, the Bornean ferret-badger never hibernates, foraging through freezing midnight downpours under a starkly contrasted black-and-white face mask.
Roloway monkey: Distinguished by a magnificent, pointed white wizard's beard up to four inches long and a matching crown fringe shaped like a tiara, the West African Roloway monkey is one of the most regal primates on Earth.
A master of interspecies teamwork, the Roloway monkey regularly forms mixed-species patrols with Diana monkeys and red colobus monkeys to double the number of eyes watching for crowned eagles.

To avoid competing with a Roloway monkey's travel partners in the same tree, Roloway monkeys specialize in peeling bark to hunt insects and eating mature seeds while neighboring monkeys take the ripe fruit.
Inside a Roloway monkey's mouth are expandable cheek pouches that can hold an entire fistful of forest berries, allowing it to grab food in dangerous open branches and chew later in hidden foliage.
Today, fewer than a few hundred Roloway monkeys survive in the wild forests of Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana, making a sighting of their white beards in the high canopy one of conservation's rarest prizes.
Manchurian hare: Unlike snowy northern hares that turn pure white in winter, the woodland Manchurian hare keeps its dappled brown-and-black camouflage coat all year long to blend into oak leaf litter.

A rare entirely jet-black morph of the Manchurian hare was once so distinctive in the Primorsky forests of the Russian Far East that 19th-century naturalists mistakenly classified it as a separate species.
Rather than digging burrows like a rabbit, the Manchurian hare rests inside a shallow depression scratched into the forest floor or hides inside hollow fallen larch trunks.
When pursued by a Siberian leopard cat or sable, a Manchurian hare weaves through dense hazel thickets and bangs its hind feet against the frozen ground to warn neighboring hares.
A Manchurian hare's ears and hind legs are noticeably shorter than those of open-steppe hares, trading top-end straight-line speed for razor-sharp cornering among tightly packed forest trees.
Banded palm civet: Across a banded palm civet's reddish-buff back run four to five bold, coal-black transverse saddles that break up its silhouette under moonlit ferns like the stripes of a miniature Tasmanian tiger.

Unlike tree-dwelling palm civets, the banded palm civet spends most of its nights prowling along rainforest stream banks, using sensitive front paws to feel under wet stones for earthworms, crickets, and freshwater snails.
The hairs along the back of a banded palm civet's neck grow pointing forward toward its head rather than backward, creating a plush, reversed-nap collar.
When startled on the forest floor, a banded palm civet arches its striped back like a Halloween cat, puffs its tail to twice its normal thickness, and hisses while stamping its front paws.
Equipped with fully retractable claws like a feline's, a climbing banded palm civet keeps its weapons razor-sharp for scrambling up vertical lianas and sleeping in high tree holes.
Six-banded armadillo: Unlike almost all other armadillos, which cannot digest fat easily and stick to ants, the six-banded armadillo stores a thick layer of subcutaneous yellow fat beneath its shell to survive lean Brazilian dry seasons.

Because a six-banded armadillo's eyes contain only rod cells and zero cone cells, it is completely colorblind and nearly blind in bright midday sun, navigating instead by a bloodhound-grade sense of smell.

When digging out a subterranean wasp or fire-ant nest, a six-banded armadillo can hold its breath for six full minutes so it never inhales choking dust or angry insects, even while furiously shoveling dirt!
After tearing into a rotting log or carrion pile, a six-banded armadillo stands up on its hind legs and balances against its stiff, armored tail like a tripod to sniff the wind for jaguars.
Though six-banded armadillos are solitary for most of the year, half a dozen individuals will suddenly gather around a single fallen palm tree or carcass to feast side by side before wandering off.
Suni: Weighing less than a gallon of milk, often just eight to ten pounds, the suni, a pint-sized East African antelope, vanishes completely inside ankle-high leaf litter on the coastal forest floor.
Beneath each of a suni's eyes sits a massive preorbital gland nearly as large as the eyeball itself, which oozes a dark, musky paste rubbed onto the tips of low twigs to mark territory.
When a crowned eagle or python approaches, the suni freezes completely motionless until the predator is within arm's reach, then explodes away in a frantic series of erratic zigzags.
Even though the suni lives in hot, humid coastal thickets from Kenya to South Africa, it requires zero standing water, getting every drop of moisture from freshly fallen leaves and fungi.
To warn its lifelong mate without giving away its exact location in the dark brush, the suni vents a faint, wheezing whistle through its nostrils that sounds like a windblown reed.
Tonkin snub-nosed monkey: Looking like an elfin cartoon character, the Tonkin snub-nosed monkey has no protruding nose bridge at all, just two upturned nostrils set flat into its face accompanied by puffy, sky-blue eye rings and thick, bright-pink lips.

According to local Vietnamese folklore in the limestone karst mountains of Ha Giang, when torrential monsoon rains fall, Tonkin snub-nosed monkeys sit in the trees with their heads tucked between their knees so rainwater doesn't drip straight into their upturned nostrils and make them sneeze!

For nearly forty years after World War II, scientists feared the flamboyant Tonkin snub-nosed monkey had gone completely extinct until a surviving population was rediscovered on steep limestone cliffs in northern Vietnam in 1989.
When a Tonkin snub-nosed monkey swings through vertical jungle canopies above razor-sharp karst pinnacles, its cream-and-black tail, longer than its entire body, acts as a fifth limb for balance.

Unlike noisy macaques, troops of Tonkin snub-nosed monkeys communicate with soft, ventriloquist-like 'hiccup' calls that echo off limestone cave walls without revealing which tree they are sitting in.
